title: 7  Dynamic panels
text:
7.5 Summary
The recipe, in five lines.

Difference, do not demean. The within estimator is biased by about \((1 + \gamma)/(T - 1)\) and more firms do not help (Nickell 1981; Croissant and Millo 2019, 165; Baltagi 2021, 188) (the bias).
Instrument the differenced lag with levels. \(y_{i,t-2}\) and earlier are valid when the shocks are serially uncorrelated (Anderson and Hsiao 1982; Baltagi 2021, 188) (difference and instrument).
Use every lag, but count them. Difference GMM with all lags, system GMM when the series is persistent, and the instrument count printed beside every estimate (difference and system GMM).
Two-step with Windmeijer standard errors. summary(robust = TRUE), never the conventional two-step covariance.
Sargan, m1, m2 and an instrument-count table. m1 must reject, m2 must not, Sargan must not (Baltagi 2021, 192); then show how γ moves as the lags change (diagnostics).

Every estimate of the persistence of employment in this chapter, on the one-lag equation and on the Arellano–Bond equation. The standard error is the one each step reported: conventional for OLS, within and Anderson–Hsiao, robust for one-step GMM, Windmeijer for two-step GMM. The Sargan p-value is given for the two-step fits, whose statistic is the one Croissant and Millo (2019, 180) describe; the instrument count includes the time dummies and the exogenous regressors.

# Plumbing: one row per fitted object from the steps above.
row_plm <- function(m, i) {
  c(coef(summary(m))[i, 1:2], sargan_p = NA, instruments = NA)
}
row_gmm <- function(m, sargan = TRUE) {
  c(coef(summary(m, robust = TRUE))[1, 1:2],
    sargan_p = if (sargan) unname(plm::sargan(m)$p.value) else NA,
    instruments = ncol(m$W[[1]]))
}
summary_tab <- rbind(
  `one-lag: pooled OLS` = row_plm(one_ols, 2),
  `one-lag: two-way within` = row_plm(one_within, 1),
  `one-lag: Anderson-Hsiao, level` = row_plm(ah_level, 1),
  `one-lag: DIF one-step` = row_gmm(one_dif1, sargan = FALSE),
  `one-lag: DIF two-step` = row_gmm(one_dif2),
  `one-lag: SYS one-step` = row_gmm(bb_one, sargan = FALSE),
  `one-lag: SYS two-step` = row_gmm(bb_two),
  `AB: pooled OLS` = row_plm(ab_ols, 2),
  `AB: two-way within` = row_plm(ab_within, 1),
  `AB: Anderson-Hsiao, levels` = row_plm(ah_two, 1),
  `AB: DIF one-step` = row_gmm(ab_one, sargan = FALSE),
  `AB: DIF two-step` = row_gmm(ab_two),
  `AB: SYS one-step` = row_gmm(ab_sys1, sargan = FALSE),
  `AB: SYS two-step` = row_gmm(ab_sys))

On the one-lag equation the consistent estimators sit inside the 0.63 to 0.96 bracket and disagree with each other by a quarter: 0.68 to 0.71 for difference GMM, 0.93 to 0.94 for system GMM, both with a Sargan p-value above 0.2. On the Arellano–Bond equation γ₁ runs from 0.47 to 1.16 across the GMM fits, and the system fit’s Sargan rejects. What the chapter can say about employment persistence in these firms is the table, not one number from it.
Limitations. Each of these has no implementation in this book’s tools and is a stated gap, with the nearest Stata benchmark named.

Kiviet’s bias-corrected within estimator (Kiviet 1995; Baltagi 2021, 188). Benchmark: Stata xtlsdvc, deferred.
The transformed likelihood of Hsiao et al. (2002) for short panels, which differences the fixed effect away and models the initial condition (Pesaran 2015, 692–93). Benchmark: Stata xtdpdqml (Kripfganz 2016), deferred.
The two-step estimator of Kripfganz and Schwarz (2019) for time-invariant regressors, and the Arellano–Bover system in its Hausman–Taylor form (Arellano and Bover 1995; Baltagi 2021, 194). Benchmark: Stata xtseqreg, deferred.
The Ahn–Schmidt nonlinear moment conditions (Ahn and Schmidt 1995; Pesaran 2015, 685): not in plm; pdynmc (Fritsch et al. 2021) runs them, shown in the Pitfalls box of step 3.
Dynamic panels with a factor error structure, where cross-sectional dependence makes the GMM estimators above inconsistent (Pesaran 2015, 696): no tool here; the CD test says whether the problem is present.
The dynamic spatial panel, with a time lag and a spatial lag together, stated as a limitation in the spatial chapter. Benchmark: Stata xsmle, model(sdpd), deferred.







Next. Back to the road map for the next question in the workflow. Everything in this chapter assumes the levels shocks are serially uncorrelated; the serial-correlation tests of the core chapter are where that assumption is checked on a static model, and m2 is where it is checked here.

title: Appendix A — Cross-sectional dependence: how much, and of what kind
text:
A.1 The two questions people confuse
Units move together. Almost always, in almost every panel. So “is there cross-sectional dependence?” is nearly never the useful question — with a large N, even an average pairwise correlation of 0.02 will reject.
The two questions that actually matter are different:
α answers the first. Everything in this note either measures it or is a coarse test whose validity is defined in terms of it.

title: Appendix A — Cross-sectional dependence: how much, and of what kind
text:
Is the co-movement pervasive? — does it involve a growing share of units, or a sparse, local handful? → this is α.
Does it have geographic structure? — is unit i correlated with its neighbours specifically? → this is the ordered family, testing for spatial dependence.
crumbs: A  Cross-sectional dependence: how much, and of what kind

title: Appendix A — Cross-sectional dependence: how much, and of what kind
text:
A.2 1. What α counts
Take a factor model where only some units load on the common shock:
\[z_{it} = a_i + \gamma_i f_t + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad
  \#\{i : \gamma_i \neq 0\} = O(N^{\alpha}).\]
α is the growth rate of the number of connected units. That is the whole idea; everything else is consequence.








α
Units sharing the shock
Picture




1
a fixed fraction of N
an oil price shock — everyone feels it


3/4
grows, but the share vanishes
a regional bloc that widens slower than the panel


1/2
about \(\sqrt{N}\)
sparse, local — a spatial weight matrix with bounded row sums



Averaging is how you see it. For the cross-section average \(\bar z_t\) (Bailey et al. 2016; Pesaran 2015b, eq. 29.6, p. 754):
\[\operatorname{Var}(\bar z_t) = \underbrace{\kappa_0 N^{2(\alpha-1)}}_{\text{co-movement}}
  + \underbrace{\kappa_1 N^{-1}}_{\text{what independence gives}}
  + O(N^{\alpha-2}), \qquad \tfrac12 < \alpha \le 1.\]
The second term is the textbook \(\sigma^2/N\). The first is the excess over it. Two readings fall straight out:

α = 1 → \(N^{0}\) → the excess never shrinks. Pooling more units never removes the common movement. This is strong dependence: common factors (Pesaran 2015b, 754).
α < 1 → the excess vanishes as \(N \to \infty\). Formally weak dependence, which is where essentially all spatial models live (Pesaran 2015b, 756, 802).







Note



Why the range is 1/2 < α ≤ 1. Below 1/2 the \(\kappa_1 N^{-1}\) term dominates the \(\kappa_0 N^{2(\alpha-1)}\) term, and α is no longer identified from the variance of the average — sparse dependence is simply indistinguishable from independence at the aggregate level. The restriction is not a technicality; it says there is nothing left to measure down there.

A.3 2. Reading α: the effective sample size
The label “weak” is asymptotic and can badly mislead in a finite panel. Set \(\kappa_0 N^{2(\alpha-1)} = \sigma^2/N_{\text{eff}}\) and you get the number that actually matters — how many independent observations your N units are worth:
\[N_{\text{eff}} \;\propto\; N^{2(1-\alpha)}\]

Read the α = 0.90 row slowly. Nine thousand individuals carry about as much cross-sectional information as six independent ones, and going from 1 000 to 9 000 units bought you two. Yet α = 0.90 is formally “weak dependence”, and a great many published panels sit near it — Bailey et al. (2016) find most macroeconomic series in roughly the 0.77–0.92 range, with equity returns essentially at 1.
So: the weak/strong dichotomy is a limit theorem. α is the finite-sample truth. That gap is the entire reason to estimate it.

title: Appendix A — Cross-sectional dependence: how much, and of what kind
section: A.4 3. What α does not tell you
text:
A.4 3. What α does not tell you
This is the easiest thing to get backwards, so state it plainly.
α says nothing about whether you need fixed effects. FE absorbs the time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity \(a_i\), and you need it for exactly the reasons you always did. What α governs is a different omitted variable: the time-varying common factor \(f_t\) with heterogeneous loadings \(\gamma_i\).
The identity that makes this click:

Two-way fixed effects is already a factor model — with \(\gamma_i = 1\) for everyone. A common time effect \(\delta_t\) absorbs a common shock only if every unit responds by the same amount.

So heterogeneous loadings are precisely the case two-way FE cannot remove, and α ≈ 1 is precisely where they bite. The correct summary:






Important



α does not tell you whether you need FE. It tells you whether FE is enough.

Low α → FE is sufficient. The omitted common shock, such as it is, washes out. Fix the standard errors and move on.
High α → FE is insufficient. \(f_t\) survives the within transformation, and if it correlates with your regressors the estimator is biased, not merely inefficient. No standard-error correction rescues a biased point estimate — not Driscoll–Kraay, not clustering, not spatial HAC. You need CCE (Pesaran 2006), explained in common factors and CCE, or interactive fixed effects.

title: Appendix A — Cross-sectional dependence: how much, and of what kind
text:
A.5 4. The CD test
Pesaran’s CD (Pesaran 2004; Pesaran 2015b, eq. 29.76, p. 786) is the average pairwise residual correlation, scaled:
\[CD = \sqrt{\frac{2T}{N(N-1)}} \sum_{i<j} \hat\rho_{ij}
  \;\xrightarrow{d}\; N(0,1).\]
Two design choices explain everything about its behaviour.
It sums raw \(\hat\rho\), not \(\hat\rho^{\,2}\). The Breusch–Pagan LM statistic (Breusch and Pagan 1980; Baltagi 2021, 412) sums \(T\hat\rho_{ij}^{\,2}\) into a \(\chi^2\), which needs \(T \gg N\) — with large N you are accumulating \(N(N-1)/2\) strictly positive terms and it diverges. CD is exactly centred at zero under the null for any T, because \(E(\hat\rho_{ij}) = 0\) in finite samples and not merely asymptotically. That is its virtue: small T, enormous N, still valid.
Signed summation is also its fatal flaw, in two specific ways:

Sign cancellation. Dependence whose pairwise correlations average to zero is invisible, however strong each individual pair. Positive and negative spatial weights are the obvious case.
Demeaned residuals are dead on arrival. Two-way FE forces \(\sum_i \hat e_{it} = 0\), which drives \(\bar\rho\) to roughly \(-1/(N-1) \approx 0\) mechanically. Running global CD on two-way FE residuals and reading non-rejection as “no dependence” is an artefact of the transformation, not evidence (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.1.2.2).

The general statement of that second point is Juodis and Reese (2022): with period-specific parameters estimated rather than known, CD diverges as T grows even when the dependence has been correctly accounted for. It is an incidental parameters problem, and it applies to CCE residuals as much as to two-way FE residuals. This is the trap in §8’s defactor-then-re-diagnose sequence: the obvious diagnostic at step 3 is exactly the one that is invalid there. On US house prices, two-way FE moves \(\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}\) only from 0.51 to 0.49 while collapsing CD from 53.3 to 0.02, p = 0.98 — see testing for CSD.
And its null is not independence. The implicit null of CD is weak dependence — α < 1/4 when N and T grow at the same rate (Pesaran 2015a; 2015b, 786). Confirmed from the other direction at (Pesaran 2015b, 839), where CD is found to be the statistic most robust to spatial alternatives — which is to say, it does not fire on them.






Warning



CD is a one-bit read on α, and a coarse one. Its size is only assured below α ≈ 1/4; the statistic starts diverging somewhere above α ≈ 1/2. In between there is a band where it is neither reliably valid nor reliably powerful. Do not read a CD rejection as “there is dependence”; read it as “there is pervasive dependence”.

All available through plm::pcdtest(test = ...).

"cd"

Large N, small T; the default first look
Dies on demeaned residuals; blind to sign cancellation


"lm"

\(T \gg N\) only

"sclm"
Scaled LM
Slightly larger N than "lm" tolerates
Still badly centred at finite T: 14.25% rejection at N=200, T=20 against a nominal 5% (Pesaran 2015b, 789)


"bcsclm"
Bias-corrected scaled LM, eq. 13.36 (Baltagi et al. 2012; Baltagi 2021, 414)
The FE-appropriate one
Requires a within model with individual or two-way effects


"rho", "absrho"
\(\bar\rho\) and \(\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}\)
Always — see §6
Not tests; no null, no p-value



If you are testing residuals from a fixed-effects model, "bcsclm" is the answer and the others are history. It exists precisely because the scaled LM’s finite-T bias, quantified above, makes it unusable at the N and T that panels actually have.

What plm does not have
Three later statistics attack CD’s blindness from different directions. None is in plm; all three are in dcce::pcd_test (Wasseja 2026).

text:
A.7 6. ρ̄ versus |ρ̄|: the poor man’s α
The last row of that table is the most useful and the most ignored. "rho" gives you \(\bar\rho\); "absrho" gives you \(\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}\). Two numbers, no null hypothesis, and together they diagnose the exact failure mode of the test sitting next to them:



Pattern
What it means
What to do




\(\bar\rho \approx \overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}\), both large
Pervasive, same-signed co-movement
You are near α = 1. Factor structure. Go to CCE.


\(\bar\rho \approx 0\), \(\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}\) large
Real dependence that cancels in sign
CD is blind here by construction. Go to the ordered tests.


both small
Little dependence of any kind
Low α. FE plus an honest vcov.



The middle row is the case where CD reports nothing and something is nonetheless badly wrong. Compute both; they cost nothing.

title: Appendix A — Cross-sectional dependence: how much, and of what kind
text:
A.8 7. If / then



If
Then




α ≈ 1, or \(\bar\rho \approx \overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}\) and large
Strong dependence. CCE (Pesaran 2006). FE is biased, not just inefficient.


α clearly below 1 and CD does not fire
Weak dependence. FE is consistent — now ask whether it is spatial (testing for spatial dependence).


α in the 0.8–0.95 middle
The modal case. Defactor first, then re-diagnose. See §8.


\(\bar\rho \approx 0\) but \(\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}\) large
Sign cancellation. Ignore CD entirely; use the ordered tests.


You only have two-way FE residuals
Global CD is uninformative by construction. Use "bcsclm", CD* (Pesaran and Xie 2021), or the randomised-W test (Millo 2017).


You have defactored (CCE, PC) residuals
Same problem, general form (Juodis and Reese 2022). CD* or CDw, never plain CD.


Dependence confirmed, structure unknown
Do not route on α alone. Corroborate with the rwtest vs pcdtest contrast (plan §5.7).

title: Appendix A — Cross-sectional dependence: how much, and of what kind
section: A.9 8. The middle is the normal case
text:
A.9 8. The middle is the normal case
Given that most real panels sit around α ≈ 0.8–0.95, the weak/strong fork is not usually a fork at all. It is a sequence, and Bailey et al. (2016) apply it that way — estimating α on the raw series and on residuals after removing factors:

Estimate α (or read \(\bar\rho\) vs \(\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}\)) on the raw series — csd_exp(use_residuals = TRUE), the Bailey et al. (2019) residual method. The Bailey et al. (2016) variable method, use_residuals = FALSE, only when the cross-section average carries the common trend; see §9.
If it points strong → defactor (CCE, or principal components).
Re-diagnose the residuals with csd_exp(use_residuals = TRUE), the Bailey et al. (2019) residual method, which is built for exactly this step. If α has dropped toward 1/2, the remaining dependence is local, and now modelling it spatially is legitimate. Do not use plain CD here — see Juodis and Reese (2022) in §4; use CD*.

Run on US house prices, the sequence gives α = 0.83 on the raw series and α = 0.51 on the CCEMG residuals, which is the clean version of this picture: the exponent α.
Fitting a spatial model to data with an unremoved common factor gets you a significant \(\hat\rho\) that is picking up the factor, not the geography. That is the single most common way this goes wrong.

title: Appendix A — Cross-sectional dependence: how much, and of what kind
text:
A.10 9. Open

An implementation now exists, and it is young. dcce::csd_exp (Wasseja 2026) implements both the Bailey et al. (2016) variable method and the Bailey et al. (2019) residual method, and it reproduces its own vignette’s α = 0.8348 for pwt8 exactly. But dcce is a single-author package first published in 2026 with no independent validation, so the α numbers here rest on one cross-check: its Pesaran CD agrees with plm::pcdtest to four decimals on the same data. Corroborate α with the rwtest vs pcdtest contrast (plan §5.7) rather than routing on it alone.
The variable method is fragile in exactly the way the theory predicts. It inverts \(\hat\alpha = 1 + \ln(\hat\sigma^2_{\bar z}) / (2\ln N)\) with a correction for the \(\kappa_1 N^{-1}\) term, and that correction scales as \(\overline{\sigma^2_i} / (2 \ln N \cdot \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar
z_t))\). When the common component does not survive averaging, the correction dominates and the estimate leaves the parameter space entirely — below 1/2 on house prices, and large and negative on an independent panel. That is the callout in §1 made visible: there really is nothing to measure down there. The package does not constrain the output to (1/2, 1], so check the number against \(\bar\rho\) before believing it.
The 1/4-to-1/2 band. The size condition α < 1/4 (Pesaran 2015b, 786) and the point at which CD starts diverging are different quantities, and the gap between them is not well characterised here. Check against Pesaran (2015a) before relying on it.

title: Appendix B — Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing
text:
B.1 Why the method exists
Regress log house prices on log income state by state and average the 49 slopes: 0.30. Add two cross-state averages to each regression and do it again: 1.14 (Holly et al. 2010; Croissant and Millo 2019, 197–99). Nothing about the data changed. What changed is that the second regression controls for a national force, interest rates and credit conditions, that moves both prices and incomes in every state, each to its own degree.
The obvious control is a year effect: a dummy for each year, which removes whatever is common to all states in that year. It fails here for one reason. A year effect removes the force only if every state feels it by the same amount. When states differ in how hard the force hits, the part of it that differs stays in the error, correlated with income, and the slope is biased. Not inefficient: biased, and no standard-error correction helps cross-sectional dependence. CCE is the fix for that case, and this note says why it works and when it does not.
crumbs: B  Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing

title: Appendix B — Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing
section: B.2 1. The model, and why year effects fail
text:
B.2 1. The model, and why year effects fail
State i in year t follows
\[
y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i x_{it} + u_{it}, \qquad
u_{it} = \lambda_i f_t + \varepsilon_{it},
\]
where \(f_t\) is the unobserved common factor, the national force, and \(\lambda_i\) is state i’s loading on it, how hard the force hits that state. The factor is also in the regressor:
\[
x_{it} = a_i + \gamma_i f_t + v_{it}.
\]
Income and the error share \(f_t\), so each state’s OLS slope picks up the factor’s effect on prices and attributes it to income. That is the leak.
A year effect subtracts the cross-state mean from every variable in every year. In the error that leaves \((\lambda_i - \bar\lambda) f_t\): the factor survives in proportion to how far each state’s loading sits from the average. Two-way fixed effects is a factor model with every loading equal to one, and it removes the factor only in that case. With heterogeneous loadings the bias stays, and α near 1 is exactly the panel where loadings are heterogeneous enough to matter (Pesaran 2015, 754).
crumbs: B  Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing

title: Appendix B — Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing
text:
B.3 2. Why averages work
Average the price equation over the N states in year t:
\[
\bar y_t = \bar\alpha + \bar\beta \bar x_t + \bar\lambda f_t
  + \bar\varepsilon_t + o_p(1),
\]
and the income equation likewise, \(\bar x_t = \bar a + \bar\gamma f_t +
\bar v_t\). As N grows the idiosyncratic averages \(\bar\varepsilon_t\) and \(\bar v_t\) vanish, and the two averages are left as two linear functions of one unknown, \(f_t\). Solve for it:
\[
f_t \approx \frac{\bar y_t - \bar\alpha - \bar\beta \bar x_t}{\bar\lambda}.
\]
The unobserved factor is, for large N, a known combination of the observed averages. So put the averages themselves into each state’s regression,
\[
y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i x_{it} + c_i \bar y_t + d_i \bar x_t + e_{it},
\]
and let each state choose its own \(c_i\) and \(d_i\). Whatever \(\lambda_i\) is, the pair \((c_i, d_i)\) can absorb \(\lambda_i f_t\), because \(f_t\) lies in the space the averages span. The factor is controlled for without being estimated, and without assuming anything about its time path. That is the whole of Pesaran (2006), and it survives factors that wander like random walks (Kapetanios et al. 2011), which is why the method is safe on price levels.
With m factors and k regressors there are \(k + 1\) averages, and they span the factors only if \(m \le k + 1\) and the \((k+1) \times m\) matrix of average loadings has full column rank: the rank condition (Pesaran 2006). One regressor buys at most two factors.
crumbs: B  Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing

title: Appendix B — Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing
text:
B.4 3. CCEMG and CCEP
Two ways to turn 49 augmented regressions into one slope (Pesaran 2015, 767–68).
CCEMG, mean group, runs the augmented regression state by state and averages the slopes:
\[
\hat\beta_{\text{CCEMG}} = \frac1N \sum_{i=1}^N \hat\beta_i, \qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}} = \frac{1}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i=1}^N
  (\hat\beta_i - \hat\beta_{\text{CCEMG}})^2 .
\]
The variance is the dispersion of the 49 slopes: no assumption about the errors within a state enters it, and it is honest about heterogeneous slopes, which is why the stripchart in the step is the estimate’s own picture.
CCEP, pooled, imposes one slope on every state while keeping the state-specific \(\alpha_i\), \(c_i\) and \(d_i\), and estimates it by least squares on the augmented data. Its variance is a sandwich that allows the true slopes to differ across states by random amounts (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 8.3.2.2). Under one common slope CCEP is the more efficient of the two. When the slopes differ, both estimate their mean, and CCEMG does so without weighting states by how much their income varies.
Read them together. CCEMG 1.14 and CCEP 1.20, each with a standard error of 0.2, are one number: the spread in the state slopes is noise around a common value, and the pooled estimate can be reported (Croissant and Millo 2019, 199). Had they been far apart, the slopes would be genuinely heterogeneous and CCEMG would be the one to report.
crumbs: B  Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing

title: Appendix B — Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing
section: B.5 4. What CCE does not fix
text:
B.5 4. What CCE does not fix

Factors that average out. If the loadings on a factor average to zero across states, \(\bar\lambda = 0\), the averages do not carry it and the rank condition fails. Pesaran (2006) shows the estimators can survive this when the loadings are independent of the regressors’ loadings, but nothing in the output says whether that holds.
More factors than averages. With one regressor and three factors the averages span two of them. The remedy is more averages, of variables that load on the missing factors even if they are not in the regression, which plm::pcce does not provide. The exponent on the CCE residuals is the check: if it is still near 1, a factor was missed (the exponent α).
A lagged dependent variable. With \(y_{i,t-1}\) on the right, the augmented regression is biased at short T, and Chudik and Pesaran (2015) add lags of the averages to repair it. Dynamic panels are a later part of time dependence.
Weak dependence. When α is near ½ the averages carry nothing and CCE changes nothing. The dependence that remains is local, and a spatial model is the tool (does it follow the map).
Interactive fixed effects (Bai 2009) estimate the factors and loadings by principal components instead of proxying them. They need the number of factors chosen in advance and more of T; CCE needs neither, which is why this book uses CCE first.
crumbs: B  Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing

title: Appendix B — Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing
text:
B.6 5. If / then



If
Then




α ≈ 1, or CD rejects on the raw series
Year effects are not enough. CCE (Pesaran 2006).


CCEMG and CCEP agree within a standard error
One common slope. Report CCEP, keep CCEMG as the check (Croissant and Millo 2019, 199).


CCEMG and CCEP differ by more than that
Heterogeneous slopes. Report CCEMG; its variance is the dispersion of the slopes.


α on the CCE residuals is still near 1
A factor was missed: more factors than averages. State it as a limitation.


The series wander
CCE still holds (Kapetanios et al. 2011). Test the residuals for a unit root (tests that allow a common factor).


A lagged outcome is a regressor
Short-T bias. Lags of the averages (Chudik and Pesaran 2015), not plain CCE.
crumbs: B  Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing

title: Appendix B — Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing
text:
B.7 6. Open

The number of factors is never tested here. The rank condition is assumed, and the only check is the exponent on the residuals, which can say that something was missed but not what.
Rank-condition failure. The conditions under which CCE survives it are in Pesaran (2006) and are not verified for the house-price panel.
Heterogeneous slopes in CCEP. The sandwich variance assumes the slope deviations are random and independent of the regressors; the step does not test it.

title: Appendix B — Common factors and CCE: what cross-section averages are doing
text:

Panel unit roots takes the CCE residuals to the next question, whether price and income share one trend. Testing for spatial dependence takes the other branch, where the averages carry nothing and the map carries everything.

title: Appendix C — Spatial weights
text:
C.1 Why there has to be a matrix
Time has an order and a direction: 1999 comes before 2000, and the past can move the future but not the reverse. A cross-section of states has neither. Arizona is not “before” Nevada, and if Nevada’s prices move Arizona’s, Arizona’s move Nevada’s in the same year. To say anything about dependence across units, the analyst has to supply the order that time supplies for free: a statement of which units are close to which, and how close. That statement is the spatial weights matrix W, N × N, with \(w_{ij}\) the weight of unit j in unit i’s row and zeros on the diagonal.
Nothing in the data produces W. It is chosen, and Anselin (1988, 19) calls that choice “one of the most controversial subjects in spatial econometrics”. Every estimate in this chapter is an estimate given W.

title: Appendix C — Spatial weights
section: C.2 1. Three ways to say neighbour
text:
C.2 1. Three ways to say neighbour
Contiguity. \(w_{ij} = 1\) when i and j share a border, 0 otherwise; “queen” contiguity counts a shared corner as a border, “rook” does not. This is usaw49 for the states and riceww for the farms, where the border is “same village”. Binary contiguity imposes the least structure, makes \(Wy\) the plain average of the neighbours, and is the usual choice when the aim is to test for spatial effects rather than to estimate a theoretically given process (Anselin 1988, 21; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.2).
Nearest neighbours. \(w_{ij} = 1\) for the k units closest to i. Every unit gets exactly k neighbours, which keeps W balanced where units differ wildly in size, at the price of links that cross no border, as the long lines in the West of the weights section show.
Distance. \(w_{ij} = 1\), or \(1/d_{ij}\), for every j within a cutoff of i, so that influence fades with distance and the cutoff says where it stops. Dense where units are small, thin where they are large.
Whichever is chosen, the chapter assumes that W is exogenous and fixed over time. Geography is exogenous; a matrix of bilateral trade shares, built from the same economy as the outcome, is not (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.2). The distance need not be geographic: a space of economic or demographic characteristics works the same way, as long as it is not an outcome of the model.

title: Appendix C — Spatial weights
section: C.3 2. Row standardisation and what ρ means
text:
C.3 2. Row standardisation and what ρ means
Dividing each row by its sum makes \(\sum_j w_{ij} = 1\), and then
\[
(Wy)_i = \sum_j w_{ij}\, y_j
\]
is the average outcome of i’s neighbours. The spatial parameter ρ then reads as a share: ρ = 0.65 on the defactored house-price residuals means a state’s residual carries 0.65 of its neighbours’ average residual. Two costs. W stops being symmetric: Maine has one neighbour and gives it weight 1; New Hampshire has three and gives Maine 1/3. And ρ stops being comparable across matrices: with four nearest neighbours every weight is 0.25, with a distance band the average weight is whatever the density makes it, and the same data return a different ρ̂ under each. The chapter reports every ρ̂ as a number for usaw49.

title: Appendix C — Spatial weights
text:
C.4 3. The parameter space
A spatial lag or error model has to invert \(I - \rho W\). The inverse exists whenever ρ is not the reciprocal of an eigenvalue of W, so the admissible interval around zero runs from \(1/\omega_{\min}\) to \(1/\omega_{\max}\), with ω the real eigenvalues. For a row-standardised W, \(\omega_{\max} = 1\), so the upper bound is 1; the lower bound is whatever the most negative eigenvalue gives, −1.39 for usaw49.
A bound that needs no eigenvalues is (Kelejian and Prucha 2010; Pesaran 2015, 799)
\[
|\rho| < \frac{1}{\tau^*}, \qquad
\tau^* = \min\big(\lVert W\rVert_1, \lVert W\rVert_\infty\big),
\]
the smaller of the largest column sum and the largest row sum. With rows standardised, \(\lVert W\rVert_\infty = 1\) and so \(\tau^* \le 1\): any \(|\rho| < 1\) is safe. The familiar statement “ρ lies in (−1, 1)” is exact only when W is row and column standardised (Pesaran 2015, 802), and usaw49’s column sums run from 0.33 to 1.7.
The eigenvalues matter for a second reason. The likelihood of every model in this chapter carries \(\ln|I - \rho W| = \sum_i \ln(1 - \rho\,\omega_i)\), and spml’s default method = "eigen" computes exactly that sum at every step of the optimiser. For N in the thousands the eigenvalues are too expensive, and the sparse-matrix and Chebyshev approximations take over (Millo and Piras 2012, sec. 5.2).

title: Appendix C — Spatial weights
section: C.5 4. Granularity: why a lag is endogenous
text:
C.5 4. Granularity: why a lag is endogenous
A spatial lag \(Wy\) is endogenous, and a within fit that includes it is biased, because \(y_j\) for a neighbour j contains \(u_j\), which is correlated with \(u_i\) through the same W. Pesaran (2015, 800) make the condition precise: the covariance of \((Wy)_{it}\) with \(u_{it}\) stays away from zero only when the weights are non-granular, that is, when some \(w_{ij}\) stay bounded away from zero as N grows. If every weight were of order \(1/N\), the lag would be a cross-section average, its covariance with any one unit’s error would vanish, and there would be nothing to instrument.
This is the bridge to the previous chapter. A cross-section average is a spatial lag with a granular W, every weight \(1/N\); it proxies a factor that every unit loads on, and CCE puts it on the right-hand side as an exogenous control. A contiguity W, with a handful of weights near 1/4 in every row, is the opposite case: its lag is endogenous, the dependence it generates is weak, and α stays below 1 (Pesaran 2015, sec. 30.3.3). The largest weight in usaw49 is 1, Maine’s.

title: Appendix C — Spatial weights
section: C.6 5. Sparsity: what the model links
text:
C.6 5. Sparsity: what the model links
W is sparse: 9% of usaw49 is non-zero. The covariance of a spatial error model is not. With \(u = (I - \lambda W)^{-1}\varepsilon\),
\[
\operatorname{Var}(u) = \sigma^2 \big[(I - \lambda W)'(I - \lambda W)\big]^{-1},
\]
and the inverse of a sparse matrix is dense: 99.7% of the cells of \((I - 0.5W)^{-1}\) are non-zero. A shock in California reaches Maine, in any spatial autoregressive model, through the chain of neighbours in between (Pesaran 2015, 801). Two alternative error forms keep the covariance as sparse as W: the spatial moving average, \(u = \varepsilon +
\lambda W\varepsilon\), and the spatial error components model, \(u = W\xi +
\varepsilon\) (Pesaran 2015, eqs. 30.5–30.6). They say a shock stops at the first neighbour. Neither is implemented in splm, whose spatial.error is the autoregressive form only, so the sharpest distinction in the theory is not available to the code.

title: Appendix C — Spatial weights
text:
C.7 If / then



If
Then




The question is whether space matters at all
Binary contiguity, row-standardised (Anselin 1988, 21)


Units differ wildly in size
k nearest neighbours; say what k and why


A ρ̂ is reported above 1
The fit is broken, or W is not row-standardised; check \(\lVert W\rVert_\infty\)

They are not comparable; compare the impacts instead (effects)

It is endogenous; the chapter’s estimators do not apply

The lag is a cross-section average, and the question is a factor, not space

title: Appendix D — Testing for spatial dependence
text:
D.1 Two families of test
The tests for cross-sectional dependence split by whether the units are ordered (Pesaran 2015, 784). The CD test, the LM tests and the exponent α treat the units as an unordered set: they ask whether the units move together, and how pervasively, without a notion of who is near whom. On a map they detect whether anything exists, never whether it has spatial structure.
That is not a small gap. The implicit null of the CD test is weak dependence, α below 1/4 when N and T grow together (Pesaran 2015, 786), and spatial processes generate weak dependence (Pesaran 2015, sec. 30.3.3). From the other side, Pesaran (2015, 839) find the CD test to be the panel unit-root diagnostic most robust to spatial alternatives, which is to say it does not fire on them. A spatial panel can pass the CD test and still be spatially dependent in every residual. The ordered family exists for that case.

title: Appendix D — Testing for spatial dependence
text:
D.2 1. The ordered statistics
Put the map in. Pesaran (2015, eqs. 30.40–30.41) give two forms. The first is Moran’s I on the panel,
\[
CD_{\text{Moran}} = \frac{\sum_t \sum_{i \ne j} w_{ij}\, \hat u_{it}\hat u_{jt}}
  {\sqrt{\,\cdot\,}},
\]
the covariance of each residual with its neighbours’ average, scaled to a standard normal (Kelejian and Prucha 1998). For large N it is equivalent to the Lagrange multiplier test of Burridge (1980), which is the lme statistic of the lag-or-error section. The second is the local CD statistic: the CD average restricted to pairs that W links, with the weights kept,
\[
CD_{P,\text{local}} = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\sum_{i<j} w_{ij}}}\
  \sum_{i<j} w_{ij}\,\hat\rho_{ij}.
\]
What plm implements as pcdtest(w = ) is the binary version: w is passed through as.logical(), so every non-zero cell becomes 1 and the statistic averages the correlations of the linked pairs with equal weight (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.1.2.1). It tests the neighbourhood structure. The weighted form of eq. 30.41 and \(CD_{\text{Moran}}\) are not implemented in this book’s tools.

title: Appendix D — Testing for spatial dependence
section: D.3 2. Why local CD over-reads a factor
text:
D.3 2. Why local CD over-reads a factor
Local CD inherits the CD test’s virtue, exact centring for any T, and adds one of its own: it has power on cross-sectionally demeaned data, where global CD is dead by construction (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.1.2.2). It also has a specific blind spot. If a factor moves every unit, every pair of units is correlated, neighbours included. Local CD then averages “a subset of spatially related pairs from a population of correlated ones”, and rejects, favouring a spatial reading of what is not spatial (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.1.2.2). On the raw house-price index it gives z = 37, with the national force still in the data; on the CCEMG residuals it gives z = 28, with the force out. Only the second number is evidence about geography, and nothing in the first number says so.

title: Appendix D — Testing for spatial dependence
text:
D.4 3. The randomised-W test
Millo (2017) turns the blind spot into a test. Under the null that the map does not matter, the units are exchangeable: hand each state a random set of “neighbours” by permuting the order of the units, and the local statistic should look the same. Compute it under B shuffled maps, \(\tau_1,
\dots, \tau_B\), and compare with the value under the true map, τ. The one-sided pseudo-p-value, for the usual alternative of positive spatial dependence, is (Croissant and Millo 2019, eq. 10.1)
\[
p^{+} = \frac{1 + \sum_{h=1}^{B} \mathbf{1}[\tau_h \ge \tau]}{B + 1};
\]
the two-sided version takes absolute values of cross-sectionally demeaned data, and the asymmetric version counts each tail separately (Croissant and Millo 2019, eqs. 10.2–10.3). rwtest defaults to alternative = "twosided" and to test = "rho", the average correlation of the linked pairs; "cd" and "sclm" use the local CD and scaled-LM statistics instead.
The test is robust to what local CD is not. A factor moves the whole distribution of shuffled statistics, true map included, so it cancels in the comparison; serial correlation does the same. That is why Croissant and Millo (2019, sec. 10.1.2.2) run it on the MG residuals, with the factor still in them, and get the same p = 0.002 as on the raw index. It is the test that displaces local CD as the primary tool, and local CD becomes the statistic that the shuffle is applied to.
Its limits are the ones its construction implies. With B = 999 the smallest p-value is 0.001 and the pile has 999 points; with the default B = 99 it is coarse. It reads W through as.logical() like pcdtest, so it never tests a weighting scheme. And it tests one order of neighbourhood at a time; order = 2 shuffles the second-order map.

title: Appendix D — Testing for spatial dependence
section: D.5 4. Before and after the fit
text:
D.5 4. Before and after the fit
The same two tests serve twice (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.1.2). On the raw data, or on residuals from which a factor has been removed, they say whether a spatial model is called for. On the residuals of the spatial model, they say whether it did its job. The second use has a trap. A spatial error model’s residuals \(u = y - X\hat\beta\) are spatially correlated by construction: the model says \(u = (I - \lambda
W)^{-1}\varepsilon\), so a residual test on \(u\) rejects whenever the model is right. What the model claims to be free of spatial correlation is \(\varepsilon = (I - \hat\lambda W)u\), period by period, and that is what the check must test. On the transformed house-price panel the local CD of \(u\) is 32 and that of \(\varepsilon\) is 0.5; on rice, 47 and −0.5. A spatial lag model’s residuals \(y - \hat\rho Wy - X\hat\beta\) are already the innovations, and need no filter.

title: Appendix E — Spatial model choice
text:
E.1 Two claims about the world
A spatial lag says that a neighbour’s outcome moves yours: a tax rate set with an eye on the next state’s, a disease that spreads, a price that buyers compare across a border. A spatial error says that only the shocks are shared: the weather that hits a whole valley, a measurement error that is local, a variable the model left out that happens to cluster on the map. The first is a mechanism; the second is a nuisance that has to be allowed for, or, as Holly et al. (2010) read it for house prices, the diffusion of a shock that is itself worth measuring (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.2.2). They are not two ways to fit one curve. They are different statements about what would happen if one unit’s outcome were changed, and the effects note spells out the difference.

title: Appendix E — Spatial model choice
text:
E.2 1. The specifications
Stack the N units of period t (Pesaran 2015, eqs. 30.1–30.9; Baltagi 2021, 401–6):








Name
Equation
Claim




SAR, spatial lag
\(y_t = \rho W y_t + X_t\beta + u_t\)
outcomes move outcomes


SEM, spatial error
\(y_t = X_t\beta + u_t,\ u_t = \lambda W u_t + \varepsilon_t\)
shocks are shared


SARAR
both, with \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) possibly different
both


SDM, Durbin
\(y_t = \rho W y_t + X_t\beta + W X_t\theta + u_t\)
neighbours’ regressors matter too



The reduced forms say what each does to an estimate. Under SAR, \(y_t = (I - \rho W)^{-1}(X_t\beta + u_t)\): \(Wy_t\) contains \(u_t\) and is endogenous, so least squares on it, pooled or within, is inconsistent (Pesaran 2015, 800; Baltagi 2021, 401). Under SEM, \(u_t = (I - \lambda W)^{-1}\varepsilon_t\): the regressors stay exogenous, and least squares is consistent and merely inefficient, with standard errors that are wrong. Pesaran (2015, 801) put the consequence in one line: under spatial errors, fixed and random effects are \(\sqrt{NT}\)-consistent, and spatial modelling buys efficiency, not consistency.
The Durbin term \(WX_t\) costs nothing in estimation: \(WX_t\) is as exogenous as \(X_t\), and splm::slag() adds it to any formula. What it changes is the reading of the coefficients, since the effect of \(x_k\) on unit i now runs through \(\beta_k\) and \(\theta_k\) together (Baltagi 2021, 406; LeSage and Pace 2009, sec. 2.7).

title: Appendix E — Spatial model choice
text:
E.3 2. The Lagrange multiplier battery
The tests of Anselin et al. (1996) need only the non-spatial fit. With residuals e, the error test is
\[
LM_\lambda = \frac{(e'We/\hat\sigma^2)^2}{T_W}, \qquad
T_W = \operatorname{tr}(W'W + W^2),
\]
and the lag test replaces \(e'We\) with \(e'Wy\) and \(T_W\) with a term that also involves the fitted values. Each is \(\chi^2_1\) under its null, and each rejects under the other’s alternative, because an omitted lag leaves spatially correlated residuals and an omitted error makes \(Wy\) look informative. The robust versions subtract from each statistic the part the other effect would contribute (Anselin et al. 1996, eqs. 10, 13):
\[
RLM_\lambda =
  \frac{\big(e'We/\hat\sigma^2 - T_W\, \tilde J^{-1}\, e'Wy/\hat\sigma^2\big)^2}
       {T_W\,(1 - T_W \tilde J^{-1})},
\]
with \(\tilde J\) the information term of the lag test. The adjustment is exact for a local departure, a small value of the other parameter, and “can behave suboptimally” when both effects are large (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.3.4.2). The reading rule that follows is in two parts. When a plain test rejects and its robust version does not, the signal was the other effect’s shadow, which is the rice case: lml = 39, rlml = 0.17. When both robust tests reject strongly, the tests have left their design range, which is the house-price case: rlml = 32, rlme = 28. The answer then comes from the fits.
slmtest implements the four for a pooled model, which is what Anselin et al. (1996) derived. With unit effects, pass model = "within" or demean the variables with plm::Within() in the formula; the lag-or-error section does both.

title: Appendix E — Spatial model choice
section: E.4 3. The encompassing model as arbiter
text:
E.4 3. The encompassing model as arbiter
When the robust tests do not settle it, fit SARAR and read it two ways (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.3.4.2). A Wald z on each spatial parameter needs no robustification, since the other effect is in the model. A likelihood ratio between SARAR and the nested SAR or SEM, \(2[\ln L_{\text{SARAR}} - \ln L_{\text{SEM}}] \sim \chi^2_1\), asks whether the lag adds anything given the error, and the reverse. On rice with random effects the lag given the error has p = 0.91: the error is the whole story.
The arbiter has one weakness. With the same W in both places, a SARAR model is close to unidentified: a positive error and a negative lag can reproduce the covariance of a plain SEM, and the two parameters trade off against each other with large standard errors (Elhorst 2014, ch. 2; LeSage and Pace 2009, ch. 2). The transformed house-price panel shows it, with a lag of −0.52 and an error of 0.87 where the separate fits gave 0.65 and 0.69. In that case the encompassing model reports two numbers that mean less than either separate one, and the honest write-up gives SEM and SAR side by side with their impacts.

title: Appendix E — Spatial model choice
section: E.5 4. The unit effect’s own spatial structure
text:
E.5 4. The unit effect’s own spatial structure
With random effects there is a further choice (Baltagi 2021, 393–95; Pesaran 2015, 803). In Anselin’s specification the unit effect is plain and only the period shock passes through \((I - \lambda W)^{-1}\); the spillovers are time-varying. In the specification of Kapoor et al. (2007) the unit effect passes through it too, so a good farmer raises the neighbours’ output in every season; the spillovers are time-invariant as well. Baltagi et al. (2013) nest both in a model with three matrices. The two differ only through the variance ratio of the unit effect; when it is small, as on rice, the fits are the same to the second decimal, and the random-effects section shows it. Whether the unit effect may be random at all is the spatial Hausman test’s question, and its answer depends on the spatial model it is asked under: on rice it rejects under the error model and not under the lag model.

title: Appendix F — Fitting spatial panels
text:
F.1 Why least squares is not enough
A spatial error model could be fitted by least squares: the slopes would be consistent, only their standard errors wrong. A spatial lag model could not, since \(Wy\) is endogenous. Both need an estimator that knows about W, and two families supply it. Maximum likelihood writes down the joint normal density of all NT observations, with the determinant that the spatial transformation adds, and maximises it. Generalised moments uses the fact that the innovations are uncorrelated with their own spatial lags, solves a small set of moment equations for λ, and finishes with feasible GLS. The first is efficient under normality and inconsistent under heteroskedasticity of unknown form (Lin and Lee 2010; Pesaran 2015, 807); the second needs neither normality nor a determinant, and gives no standard error for the spatial parameter.

title: Appendix F — Fitting spatial panels
section: F.2 1. The likelihood and its Jacobian
text:
F.2 1. The likelihood and its Jacobian
For the pooled spatial error model, with \(B = I_N - \lambda W\) and \(u = y - X\beta\) (Anselin 1988, ch. 6; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.2.3):
\[
\ln L = -\frac{NT}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) + T\ln|B|
  - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\, u'(I_T \otimes B'B)\,u .
\]
The term \(T \ln|B| = T \sum_i \ln(1 - \lambda\omega_i)\), with ω the eigenvalues of W, is the Jacobian of the transformation from the innovations to the observed errors; without it the likelihood would push λ to the edge of its range. For the spatial lag model the transformation is on the outcome, \(A y = X\beta + u\) with \(A = I_N - \rho W\), and the Jacobian is \(T\ln|A|\). spml computes the eigenvalues once and the sum at every step of nlminb; for N in the thousands it switches to sparse or approximate determinants (Millo and Piras 2012, sec. 5).

title: Appendix F — Fitting spatial panels
section: F.3 2. Fixed effects: transformation or correction
text:
F.3 2. Fixed effects: transformation or correction
Within estimation demeans every variable by unit. For a spatial model the demeaning has a side effect: the T demeaned errors of a unit are no longer independent, so the likelihood above is misspecified on the demeaned data (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.3.1). Lee and Yu (2010) give two ways out. The first replaces demeaning with an orthonormal transformation, a matrix that removes the unit mean and leaves T − 1 uncorrelated errors behind; the estimator is then consistent and asymptotically normal when either N or T grows (Pesaran 2015, 802–3). The second keeps demeaning and corrects the error variance after the fact (Lee and Yu 2010, sec. 3.2). splm takes the second route: spml(model = "within") is the pooled fit on demeaned data with the variance corrected, and the “either N or T” property of the first route does not transfer to it. Millo and Piras (2012, sec. 8.2) check by simulation that the practical difference is small.

title: Appendix F — Fitting spatial panels
section: F.4 3. Random effects: two covariances, twelve error structures
text:
F.4 3. Random effects: two covariances, twelve error structures
With a random unit effect the error is \(u_{it} = \mu_i + v_{it}\), and the question is where W enters. In Anselin’s specification only the period shock is spatial, \(v_{\cdot t} = \lambda W v_{\cdot t} + \varepsilon_{\cdot
t}\), and with \(\phi = \sigma^2_\mu/\sigma^2_\varepsilon\) (Baltagi 2021, eq. 13.10; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.3.2.1)
\[
\Omega = \sigma^2_\varepsilon
  \big[\phi\,(J_T \otimes I_N) + I_T \otimes (B'B)^{-1}\big].
\]
In the specification of Kapoor et al. (2007) the unit effect passes through W as well, so the whole composite error is spatially filtered (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.3.2.2):
\[
\Omega = \sigma^2_\varepsilon\, (\phi J_T + I_T) \otimes (B'B)^{-1}.
\]
spml(model = "random") calls these spatial.error = "b" and "kkp". Both are cases of the error menu of spreml, which composes three letters: sem for a spatial error, sr for a serially correlated remainder, \(\varepsilon_{it} = \psi\varepsilon_{i,t-1} + \eta_{it}\), and re for the random effect. "semsrre" holds all three (Millo 2014; Baltagi et al. 2007); "semsr" drops the effect; "sem2re" is the KKP form; "ols" is a plain regression, which with lag = TRUE is the pure spatial lag of the map section. The likelihood “is not well behaved”: nlminb from zero starting values is the default, initval = "estimate" starts from the restricted fits, and a singular Hessian means a parameter is not there to estimate, as on a panel from which the unit means have already been partialled out.

title: Appendix F — Fitting spatial panels
text:
F.5 4. Generalised moments
Kelejian and Prucha (1999) estimate λ from three moment conditions on the innovations \(\varepsilon = B u\): their mean square equals \(\sigma^2\), the mean square of \(W\varepsilon\) equals \(\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(W'W)/N\), and \(\varepsilon\) and \(W\varepsilon\) are uncorrelated. Replace u by consistent residuals, solve the three equations in λ and \(\sigma^2\), and run GLS with the implied covariance. Kapoor et al. (2007) extend the conditions to six for the random-effects panel (Baltagi 2021, eq. 13.13), which can be used three ways: the first three only (moments = "initial", the default and the least efficient), all six weighted by their covariance under normality ("fullweights"), or all six with a simplified weight ("weights"). For fixed effects, Mutl and Pfaffermayr (2011) replace the OLS residuals by within two-stage least squares residuals and use the first three conditions. spgm wraps all of it, with method choosing among the within, between, GLS and error-component 2SLS estimators of Baltagi (2021, 401–4) when a lag is present. Two costs: no standard error for λ, so no significance test on it, and with a single regressor the summary() method of splm 1.6-5 fails, so the fit is read from coef() and $rho.

title: Appendix F — Fitting spatial panels
section: F.6 5. The tests that need only the restricted model
text:
F.6 5. The tests that need only the restricted model
Three families of Lagrange multiplier test fit from the OLS residuals, so that the expensive model is estimated only once a test has asked for it.
Lag against error. The four statistics of Anselin et al. (1996), in the choice note.
Random effect and spatial error. Baltagi et al. (2003) derive the joint test of \(\sigma^2_\mu = 0\) and λ = 0 (LMH), the marginal tests of each (LM1, LM2), and the conditional tests of each allowing the other (CLMmu, CLMlambda); the conditional ones are the ones to read, since the joint test rejects for either reason (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 10.3.4.1).
Random effect, spatial error and serial correlation. Baltagi et al. (2007) add ψ as a third symptom, with a joint test J and the three conditional tests C.1 (λ given the other two), C.2 (ψ given the other two) and C.3 (\(\sigma^2_\mu\) given the other two). Each conditional test fits the model with the other two effects and tests the third from its score, which is why C.2 on rice takes a few seconds. Testing for any one of the three while ignoring the other two “leads to misleading results”; the full semsrre fit then puts magnitudes beside the tests.
Fixed against random. The spatial Hausman test of Mutl and Pfaffermayr (2011) compares the random-effects GLS slopes with the within slopes,
\[
H = (\hat\beta_{RE} - \hat\beta_{FE})'\,
    [\widehat V_{FE} - \widehat V_{RE}]^{-1}\,
    (\hat\beta_{RE} - \hat\beta_{FE}) \sim \chi^2_k ,
\]
(Millo and Piras 2012, eq. 32). sphtest fits both from a formula, by ML with errors = "BSK" or "KKP", or by GM with no error structure to choose; or takes two fitted objects. The statistic is conditional on the spatial model passed as spatial.model: on the rice panel it rejects random effects under the error model, χ² = 31, and does not under the lag model, χ² = 0.6. The verdict that counts is the one under the model the choice note selected.

title: Appendix G — Direct and indirect effects
text:
G.1 The question a reader of an impact evaluation asks
If Ohio’s income rose by 10% and nothing else changed, by how much would Ohio’s house prices rise? In a plain regression the answer is β, and the reader is done. In a spatial lag model it is not, because the model says Ohio’s price depends on Pennsylvania’s, Pennsylvania’s on Ohio’s, and the rise goes round that loop before it settles. A paper that fits \(y = \rho W y + X\beta + u\) and reports β as “the effect of income” has not reported an effect of anything (LeSage and Pace 2009, ch. 2).

title: Appendix G — Direct and indirect effects
text:
G.2 1. The reduced form
Solve the lag model for y, for one period:
\[
y = (I - \rho W)^{-1} X\beta + (I - \rho W)^{-1} u.
\]
The matrix \((I - \rho W)^{-1}\) is the sum \(I + \rho W + \rho^2 W^2 +
\dots\), which converges whenever ρ is inside the parameter space of the weights note. Its terms are the loop: the first is the own effect, the second the neighbours’, the third the neighbours’ neighbours’, and so on without end. Differentiating with respect to regressor k in every unit at once gives an N × N matrix of partial effects (LeSage and Pace 2009, eq. 2.49)
\[
S_k = \frac{\partial y}{\partial x_k'} = (I - \rho W)^{-1}\beta_k ,
\]
whose \((i, j)\) cell is the effect of \(x_k\) in unit j on y in unit i. β is the value every cell would take if ρ were zero.

title: Appendix G — Direct and indirect effects
text:
G.3 2. Three averages
N² numbers per regressor are too many to report. LeSage and Pace (2009, sec. 2.7) reduce them to three:

the direct effect, the average diagonal cell, \(\bar S_k^{\,d} = N^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(S_k)\): a unit’s own response, including what comes back to it through its neighbours;
the total effect, the average row sum, \(\bar S_k^{\,t} = N^{-1}\iota' S_k\, \iota\): the response of a typical unit when \(x_k\) rises in every unit;
the indirect effect, their difference: what a typical unit receives from everyone else, or equivalently what a change in one unit sends to all the others, since the average row sum and the average column sum of \(S_k\) are the same number.

With a row-standardised W the row sums of \((I - \rho W)^{-1}\) all equal \(1/(1-\rho)\), so the total effect is \(\beta_k / (1 - \rho)\): the spatial multiplier. With ρ = 0.65 on house prices the multiplier is 2.8, and an income slope of 0.72 becomes a total effect of 2.0. The direct effect exceeds β by the feedback, \(\beta_k[N^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(I - \rho
W)^{-1} - 1]\), which is 0.11 on house prices and 0.01 on rice.

title: Appendix G — Direct and indirect effects
text:
G.4 3. Standard errors
Each average is a nonlinear function of ρ and β, so its standard error is not read off the coefficient table. LeSage and Pace (2009, sec. 5.2) draw (ρ, β) from the estimated asymptotic normal distribution, recompute the three averages for each draw, and take the dispersion; 200 draws give two decimals. With large N the inverse is replaced by traces of powers of W, \(\operatorname{tr}(W^q)\), computed once by spatialreg::trW, which is what type = "MC" and "moments" do in impacts(). The "moments" route needs a symmetric W, or the similar symmetric matrix of a row-standardised one.

text:

The spatial error model has no indirect effects at all, which is the other half of the choice note: a reader who wants spillovers has to have put a lag in. The Durbin term breaks the shortcut \(\beta_k / (1 - \rho)\), and makes the ratio of indirect to direct effects differ across regressors (Baltagi 2021, 406; LeSage and Pace 2009, sec. 2.7).

title: Appendix H — Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth
text:
H.1 Why pool at all
A single unit-root test on 20 or 30 annual observations has almost no power: the Dickey–Fuller distribution is wide, and a root of 0.9 looks much like a root of 1 over that span. Panel tests buy power by adding units instead of years. N series of length T carry more evidence against a unit root than one series of length T, provided the series bring independent evidence.
That proviso is the whole subject of this note. The extra power comes from averaging, and averaging only helps when the things averaged are not the same thing counted twice. Everything below is a consequence of asking what is being averaged, and over what.
crumbs: H  Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth

title: Appendix H — Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth
text:
H.2 1. One null, three alternatives
Every test in plm::purtest and plm::cipstest, except Hadri’s, shares one null. Write each unit’s ADF regression as
\[\Delta y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i y_{i,t-1}
  + \sum_{j=1}^{p_i} \gamma_{ij} \Delta y_{i,t-j} + \varepsilon_{it},
  \qquad \beta_i = \rho_i - 1.\]
The null is \(H_0: \beta_i = 0\) for every i. The tests differ in what they claim when they reject (Pesaran 2015, 818–20, eqs. 31.4–31.6):










Alternative
In words
Tests




H₁ₐ
\(\beta_i = \beta < 0\) for all i
one common stationary root
LLC, Harris–Tzavalis, Breitung


H₁b
\(\beta_i < 0\) for \(N_1\) units, \(N_1/N \to \kappa > 0\)
a share of the panel is stationary
IPS, Fisher-type, CIPS


H₁c
\(\beta_i < 0\) for a fixed number of units, \(\kappa = 0\)
a handful is stationary
none



H₁ₐ is strong: it says every unit reverts, and at the same speed. Few economists believe that of 49 states or 170 regions, which is why the heterogeneous alternative H₁b became the default after Im et al. (2003).
H₁c is the case no averaging test can see. With a fixed count of stationary units, their signal is divided by an N that keeps growing. The simulation in the examples shows it: IPS power against two stationary series falls from 0.40 to 0.25 as N goes from 10 to 90, while power against a 40% share rises to 1.






Important



The printed p-value does not carry the alternative. purtest labels the alternative “stationarity” for LLC and IPS alike, though LLC rejects towards H₁ₐ and IPS towards H₁b. The alternative has to be written into the text by hand, every time a panel unit-root result is reported.


Remark 8 of Pesaran (2015, 820) sets the limit on that text. When T is short — around 15 — a panel rejection is informative only “in an average sense”. It says the panel, taken as a whole, does not look like N random walks. It does not say which units are stationary.
crumbs: H  Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth

title: Appendix H — Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth
section: H.3 2. How the first generation builds a statistic
text:
H.3 2. How the first generation builds a statistic
Each first-generation test runs the ADF regression above on every unit and then combines the results. They differ only in what they combine.









Family
What it combines
Tests in plm
Source




Pooled
one \(\hat\beta\) from all units stacked
"levinlin"
Levin et al. (2002)


Mean of t
the average of the N ADF t statistics
"ips"
Im et al. (2003)


Fisher
the N individual p-values
"madwu", "Pm", "invnormal", "logit"
Maddala and Wu (1999), Choi (2001)


Reversed null
the N KPSS statistics
"hadri"
Hadri (2000)



Pooled. LLC stacks all units and estimates one \(\beta\). Pooling only makes sense if \(\beta\) is common, so LLC’s alternative is H₁ₐ by construction. The pooled t is biased because each unit has its own intercept and lag structure, and Levin et al. (2002) correct it with tabulated mean and variance adjustments (Baltagi 2021, 340–43). Harris–Tzavalis (Harris and Tzavalis 1999) and Breitung (Breitung 2000) are in the same family. Neither is in plm.
Mean of t. IPS averages the individual ADF statistics, \(\bar t = N^{-1}\sum_i t_i\), then standardises (Baltagi 2021, 344–45). Each unit keeps its own \(\beta_i\), so the alternative is H₁b. The unstandardised tbar is exact for fixed T but is read against tabulated critical values, and only without lags.
Fisher. Maddala and Wu (1999) combine the individual p-values instead of the statistics: under the null, \(-2\sum_i \ln p_i \sim \chi^2_{2N}\). Choi (2001) adds three variants. "invnormal" sums \(\Phi^{-1}(p_i)\), "logit" sums \(\ln[p_i/(1-p_i)]\), and "Pm" standardises the Maddala–Wu statistic so that it stays valid as \(N \to \infty\). The Fisher family needs neither a balanced panel nor equal lag lengths, which is why it runs on EmplUK where LLC refuses (Baltagi 2021, 346–48).
A Fisher test is only as good as its p-values, and those come from the non-standard Dickey–Fuller distribution. plm reads them off the response surfaces of MacKinnon (1996) through urca (Pfaff 2008). Without urca it falls back to the older approximation of MacKinnon (1994). On US house prices the switch moves the Maddala–Wu p-value from 0.4292 to 0.4313 — visible in the fourth decimal, irrelevant to a reading.
Reversed null. Hadri (2000) tests the opposite hypothesis: every series is stationary, against a unit root in at least one. It is the panel version of the KPSS test (Kwiatkowski et al. 1992), an LM statistic averaged over units. Its value is corroboration. When LLC, IPS and Maddala–Wu fail to reject a unit root and Hadri rejects stationarity, two tests with opposite nulls point the same way. That is the pattern on log house prices: p = 0.10, 0.43 and 0.78 for the first three, p ≈ 0 for Hadri.
Lag length. Every test except Hadri needs the \(p_i\) lags of the ADF regression. purtest fixes them by hand or chooses them per unit by AIC, SIC, or the general-to-specific rule of Hall (1994). Too few lags leave serial correlation in \(\varepsilon_{it}\) and over-reject. Too many waste the short T the panel was meant to compensate for.

title: Appendix H — Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth
section: H.4 3. First and second generation: one assumption
text:
H.4 3. First and second generation: one assumption
“Second generation” is not a date. It is one assumption dropped: that units are independent once a common time effect is removed.
The first generation allows exactly one form of dependence. Subtract the cross-section mean each period and a common shock that hits every unit equally disappears. That is the two-way fixed-effects identity of cross-sectional dependence: a time effect is a factor model with every loading equal to one. If the loadings differ, demeaning leaves the factor in the residuals and every unit’s evidence is partly the same evidence.
Pesaran’s CADF regression (Pesaran 2007) allows heterogeneous loadings. It adds the cross-section averages \(\bar y_{t-1}\) and \(\Delta \bar y_t\) to each unit’s ADF equation:
\[\Delta y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i y_{i,t-1} + c_i \bar y_{t-1}
  + d_i \Delta \bar y_t + \dots + e_{it}.\]
The averages proxy the single unobserved factor, and each unit gets its own coefficients on them, so each unit gets its own loading. CIPS is the mean of the resulting t statistics — IPS on defactored regressions (Baltagi 2021, 352–53). The idea is the same one that drives CCE estimation, in common factors and CCE.
plm::cipstest exposes all three levels of this argument through model:








model =
Regression
Handles




"mg"
plain ADF per unit, averaged
independence only — this is IPS


"dmg"
ADF on cross-sectionally demeaned data
one factor, equal loadings


"cmg" (default)
CADF, with cross-section averages
one factor, any loadings



Nothing in plm handles more than one factor. Pesaran et al. (2013) extend CIPS by adding further cross-section averages of other variables, and add the CSB statistic (Pesaran 2015, 836). Moon–Perron (Moon and Perron 2004), Bai–Ng’s PANIC (Bai and Ng 2004) and Phillips–Sul (Phillips and Sul 2003) defactor by principal components first and test afterwards. None has an R implementation in this project.
CIPS has a cost: its distribution is non-standard and depends on N, T and the deterministic terms. cipstest returns the nearest tabulated significance level, not an exact p-value. A printed p-value = 0.1 means above 0.10, and 0.01 means below 0.01.
crumbs: H  Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth

title: Appendix H — Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth
text:
H.5 4. Size before power
Every comparative ranking of these tests in the textbooks is a ranking of power — and power only means something when the test rejects a true null at its nominal rate. Both standard rankings assume that:

LLC has higher local power than IPS (Pesaran 2015, 819);
LLC and Breitung have the smallest size distortions, and Fisher does at least as well as IPS (Pesaran 2015, 838; Baltagi 2021, 348).

Two things break size in a large-N, short-T panel, and they compound.
The shape of the panel. LLC’s asymptotics need T to grow faster than N (Levin et al. 2002; Baltagi 2021, 340–43). On independent random walks, with no dependence at all, the examples’ simulation gives LLC a size of 0.09 at N/T = 0.04 and 0.855 at N/T = 3.33. IPS is better but not right: 0.085 to 0.15 at T = 30. The target shape of this project is N/T ≈ 8.5, off the end of that table.
Cross-sectional dependence. When units move together, N series are worth fewer than N independent ones, and a test that counts them as N over-rejects. Baltagi et al. (2007) ran 1600 experiments under spatial error dependence: distortions are largest under a spatial autoregressive error and grow with the density of W (Baltagi 2021, 353–54).
Pesaran (2015, 839) draws two rules from that literature, and they pull in opposite directions:

The CD-based approach (CIPS) is the most robust to spatial alternatives.
Factor-based corrections are invalid under weak dependence, because they remove a “factor” that is not there.

In the project’s own simulation, on a 7 × 7 rook W, CIPS held its size: 0.04 at λ = 0 and 0.07 at λ = 0.8. The four first-generation tests rejected a true null two and a half to twelve times too often even at λ = 0. Shape, not space, did most of the damage.






Warning



At N/T ≫ 1, a first-generation rejection is not evidence. It is what those tests do to random walks at that shape. Report CIPS, and read every first-generation p-value as an upper bound on the evidence rather than a measurement of it.
crumbs: H  Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth

title: Appendix H — Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth
text:
H.6 5. What a rejection licenses
Under H₁b, a rejection means some share of units is stationary. It does not say which, and it is not a licence to treat the panel as stationary and pool it.
Hanck (2013) turns the rejection into a list. Take the individual p-values a Fisher-type test already computes, sort them, and apply two classical multiple-testing results:

Simes’ test (Simes 1986) of the intersection null. With sorted p-values \(p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(N)}\), reject when \(\min_j N p_{(j)}/j \le \alpha\). Unlike the Fisher combination, it stays valid under general cross-sectional dependence.
Hommel’s procedure (Hommel 1988) for the individual hypotheses. It controls the family-wise error rate, so each unit is judged on its own without the multiplicity of N tests inflating false rejections.

plm::phansitest implements both. It accepts any purtest object with per-series p-values (madwu, Pm, invnormal, logit, ips) and refuses Hadri, whose statistic is not built from individual p-values.
The two cases in the examples show both outcomes:



Panel
Simes global p
Units rejected (Hommel)




19 real exchange rates (Hanck 2013, Table 11)
0.0003
10 of 19


49 US state house prices
0.12
0 of 49



The exchange-rate panel rejects the intersection null and names the ten stationary countries — the two answers Remark 8 asks for. The house-price panel rejects neither. Note that its Simes p-value of 0.12 is far sharper than the Maddala–Wu p-value of 0.43 on the same data.

title: Appendix H — Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth
section: H.7 6. The assumption no test checks
text:
H.7 6. The assumption no test checks
Cross-sectional correlation is units moving together. Cross-unit cointegration is stronger: a linear combination of different units’ series is stationary, so the units share a stochastic trend. Pesaran (2015, 836) warns that panel unit-root tests may be “severely biased” under the second while tolerating the first.
CADF allows one common I(1) factor — that is what the cross-section averages absorb — and rules out further cointegration among what is left (Pesaran 2015, 837). The subsampling test of Choi and Chue (2007) allows it but needs N small relative to T (Pesaran 2015, 838), the opposite of a spatial panel.
Correlation does not reveal it. In the examples, a cointegrated pair and a pair with correlated increments have correlations of 0.90 and 0.77. A Johansen rank test separates them perfectly; no CD statistic or α could. So every CIPS result in this book holds under an assumption the book cannot test.
crumbs: H  Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth

title: Appendix H — Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth
text:
H.8 7. If / then







If
Then




CD rejects, or α is near 1
First-generation tests are invalid. Use CIPS.


N/T well above 1
First-generation size is broken even without dependence. Use CIPS.


CIPS rejects
A share of units is stationary (H₁b). Name them with phansitest.


CIPS does not reject
Treat the panel as I(1). Corroborate with Hadri’s reversed null.


Dependence is weak and spatial, not factor-driven
CIPS defactors needlessly. Its size survived λ ≤ 0.8 here, but that is not a general licence.


Several common factors are plausible
Not testable in this book. State it as a limitation.


The text says “the panel is stationary”
Rewrite it. Say which alternative was tested, and how many units.

title: Appendix H — Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth
text:
H.9 8. Open

Missing tests. Breitung and Harris–Tzavalis — the two tests with the best size record in the comparisons — are not in purtest. The benchmark is Stata’s xtunitroot.
Several factors. CIPS with multiple factors and CSB (Pesaran et al. 2013), Moon–Perron and PANIC have no R implementation and no verification target.
Cross-unit cointegration. No panel test exists in R. The assumption has to be carried as a stated limitation into cointegration in panels.
The target shape. No published size table covers N ≈ 170, T ≈ 20 with a spatial W. The examples’ Monte Carlo is the only evidence, and it covers this code on one W.
A software trap. In plm 2.6.7, the print method of phansitest says “H0 rejected (globally)” whatever the result. Read $rejected.no and compute Simes’ p-value directly.

title: Appendix H — Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth
text:
H.10 Next
With the unit-root question settled for a panel, the next one is whether its I(1) series are cointegrated. Cointegration in panels covers it, with the code in cointegration and the long run; the only verifiable route is the CCE-plus-CIPS substitute of the second-generation section.
