crumbs: H  Panel unit roots: what a rejection is worth

title: Appendix I — Cointegration in panels
text:
I.1 Why the method exists
Log house prices and log income in a state both wander: each has a unit root, a shock that never fades, so neither returns to a fixed level (why it matters). Regress one on the other and the fit looks good. It would look good for any two wandering series, related or not. That is the spurious regression, noticed in the 1920s and shown by Monte Carlo in the 1970s: a confident t statistic between two series that have nothing to do with each other (Granger and Newbold 1974; Pesaran 2015, 26).
What rescues the regression is its residual. If prices and income share one trend, the gap between them does not wander: it is stationary, and the slope is a long-run elasticity. Two series that are each I(1), integrated of order one, stationary only after differencing, but have a stationary linear combination are cointegrated (Engle and Granger 1987; Pesaran 2015, 523). The test is to regress, take the residual, and test it for a unit root (Engle and Granger 1987; Pesaran 2015, 525). In one state over 29 years that test has almost no power: cointegration tests in a single unit are weak at short T (Baltagi 2021, 357), for the same reason the unit-root tests of the unit-root note are.
So the panel is pooled for power, and the proviso of that note returns: the states must bring independent evidence. The panel also adds a trap of its own. Stack N independent spurious regressions, and the pooled slope no longer wanders as a single spurious slope does: it converges to a long-run average, with a normal limit, whether or not any cointegration exists (Phillips and Moon 1999; Baltagi 2021, 355). Its t statistic still grows with \(\sqrt T\), so the tendency to find a relation that is not there “may be even stronger in panel data regressions than in the pure time series case” (Kao 1999; Pesaran 2015, 844). A sensible pooled slope is no evidence of a long-run relation. Only the residual is.

title: Appendix I — Cointegration in panels
section: I.2 One unit: a regression and a rank
text:
I.2 One unit: a regression and a rank
Write the cointegrating regression of state i as
\[y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i x_{it} + u_{it},\]
with \(y\) log price and \(x\) log income. The Engle–Granger test runs OLS, then a Dickey–Fuller regression on \(\hat u_{it}\) with no intercept and no trend; a rejection of the unit root is read as cointegration (Engle and Granger 1987; Pesaran 2015, 525). The critical values are not those of a unit-root test on an observed series. Under the null the regression is spurious, so the residual has a distribution of its own, tabulated for it (Phillips and Ouliaris 1990; Pesaran 2015, 525). The result also depends on which series is on the left, and the test can see at most one relation (Pesaran 2015, 525–26).
Johansen’s test removes both limits by treating the pair as a system. Stack \(z_{it} = (y_{it}, x_{it})'\), write its vector autoregression of order \(p\) in levels with coefficient matrices \(\Phi_{ij}\), and rewrite it in error correction form,
\[\Delta z_{it} = -\Pi_i z_{i,t-1}
  + \sum_{j=1}^{p-1} \Gamma_{ij} \Delta z_{i,t-j} + u_{it},
  \qquad \Pi_i = I - \sum_{j=1}^{p} \Phi_{ij},\]
the form of Pesaran (2015, 529, eq. 22.17). If \(z_{it}\) is I(1), the left side and the lagged differences are stationary, so \(\Pi_i z_{i,t-1}\) must be too, and that forces \(\Pi_i\) to have reduced rank, \(\Pi_i = \alpha_i
\beta_i'\) (Pesaran 2015, 529, eq. 22.18). The rank \(r_i\) of \(\Pi_i\) is the number of stationary combinations, and \(\beta_i\) holds them (Johansen 1988, 1991; Pesaran 2015, 529). With two series, \(r_i = 0\) means no shared trend, \(r_i = 1\) one shared trend, and \(r_i = 2\) that both series are stationary, which contradicts the unit-root result the chapter started from. The trace statistic for rank \(r\) against rank \(m\) is
\[\mathrm{LR}(H_r \mid H_m) = -T \sum_{i=r+1}^{m} \log(1 - \hat\lambda_i),\]
built from the smallest eigenvalues of the reduced-rank regression, and it does not change when the series are reordered (Johansen 1991; Pesaran 2015, 541). Its limit is a multivariate Dickey–Fuller distribution, with critical values that depend on the number of series and on whether the constant and trend are restricted to the long-run relation or left free (Pesaran 2015, 543). That choice is Johansen’s five cases (Johansen 1994; Pesaran 2015, 539); the step’s default, an unrestricted constant and no trend, is the third case, which allows a drift in the levels. The whole apparatus is asymptotic, and Monte Carlo evidence says it is reliable only when T is reasonably large and the system small (Pesaran 2015, 547). At \(T = 29\) per state, the step’s 49 ranks are a tally, not 49 verdicts.

title: Appendix I — Cointegration in panels
text:
I.3 The precondition
The panel tests below are residual tests. Pesaran (2015, 839) states the condition under which a residual test is the right tool: \(r_i = 1\) in every unit, with the variables split as \((y_{it}, x_{it}')\) and no cointegration among the regressors \(x_{it}\). A system test allows \(r_i > 1\) and needs no such split. The two also treat the residual’s serial correlation differently. Residual tests absorb it in a long-run variance, the variance a serially correlated series shows in its running sums, estimated without a model; system tests model it with the VAR’s lags (Pesaran 2015, 839). With one regressor the second half of the condition holds by default, and the first half is what the state-by-state ranks check.
The single-equation estimators of the long run share the condition. All regressors must be I(1) and not cointegrated among themselves, or the long-run variance matrix they divide by is singular; and the relation must be one that \(y_{it}\) truly enters, since it is normalised to a unit coefficient (Pesaran 2015, 852).
Why not one system for the whole panel? Stack every state’s pair into one vector and run Johansen on it, and cointegration within states and across them is covered at once, with a free error covariance for the dependence. That works when the stacked vector has fewer than about ten series and \(T > 100\) (Banerjee et al. 2004; Pesaran 2015, 839–40); the number of parameters grows with \(N^2\), so T must be far larger than N (Pesaran 2015, 855). At 98 series and \(T = 29\) it is out of reach. In practice the dependence is carried by common factors, a few unobserved series that load on every unit, each to its own degree (common factors and CCE). That is the setting of equation 31.38 in Pesaran (2015, 840), and it is where the substitute below comes from.

title: Appendix I — Cointegration in panels
text:
I.4 Four panel tests
Kao. One slope for every unit, and the error tested for a unit root with the panel pooled. Take the within residuals \(\tilde e_{it}\), the residuals of the fit with a state intercept (fixed or random), and run
\[\tilde e_{it} = \rho \tilde e_{i,t-1} + v_{it}.\]
The null of no cointegration is \(\rho = 1\) (Kao 1999; Baltagi 2021, 357). Kao builds four Dickey–Fuller statistics from \(\hat\rho\) and its t ratio, two for regressors unrelated to the error at every date and two allowing the regressors and the error to be related, plus an ADF statistic from the lag-augmented regression. Each is shifted and scaled by a mean and variance and converges to \(N(0, 1)\) in sequential limits, T first and then N (Kao 1999; Baltagi 2021, 357–58; Pesaran 2015, 848). The correction assumes the nuisance parameters are the same for every unit (Pesaran 2015, 848).
McCoskey–Kao. The reverse null. With unit-specific slopes, the error is split into a random walk and a noise term, and the null of cointegration is that the random walk has zero variance (McCoskey and Kao 1998; Baltagi 2021, 359). The statistic is the LM form
\[\mathrm{LM} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{T^2}
  \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{S_{it}^2}{\hat\sigma_e^2},
  \qquad S_{it} = \sum_{j=1}^{t} \hat e_{ij},\]
a partial sum of residuals, and \(\sqrt N (\mathrm{LM} - \mu) \to N(0,
\sigma^2)\) with moments found by simulation (McCoskey and Kao 1998; Baltagi 2021, 359). The residuals must come from an efficient estimator of the long run (Baltagi 2021, 359), and the test is the panel version of the single-series test of a stationary error (Pesaran 2015, 850). Two warnings come with it: the asymptotic approximation is often poor, and the test “is not equipped to deal with cross-sectional dependence” (Baltagi 2021, 359).
Pedroni. Unit-specific slopes, and seven statistics in two families (Pedroni 1999, 2004). The group-mean family computes a statistic unit by unit and averages, as a unit-root test against a heterogeneous alternative does; the panel family sums numerator and denominator over units before dividing, as a test against one common alternative does (Baltagi 2021, 360; Pesaran 2015, 848–49). Baltagi (2021, 360–61, eqs. 12.25–12.26) prints one of each. The group-mean \(\rho\) form is a sum of unit-by-unit Phillips–Ouliaris statistics (Phillips and Ouliaris 1990),
\[Z_{\tilde\rho} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}
  \frac{\sum_{t}(\hat e_{i,t-1}\Delta\hat e_{it} - \hat\lambda_i)}
       {\sum_{t}\hat e_{i,t-1}^2},\]
with \(\hat\lambda_i\) half the gap between the long-run and the contemporaneous variance of unit i’s residual; the panel t form sums over units first, each unit weighted by its long-run conditional variance. Each statistic is read after centring and scaling by tabulated moments, \((Z - \mu\sqrt N)/\sigma \to N(0, 1)\) (Pedroni 1999; Pesaran 2015, 849); for the model with an intercept and no trend, the panel t form obeys \(Z_{\hat t} + 1.73\sqrt N \to N(0, 0.93)\) (Baltagi 2021, 361). Averaging pieces rather than whole statistics makes a rejection hard to read; the averaged statistics have the plain reading, that enough units sit far from what the null predicts (Baltagi 2021, 361).
Larsson–Lyhagen–Löthgren. The system test. Run Johansen’s trace test in each unit, centre and scale each statistic by its tabulated mean and variance, and average. The LR-bar statistic is IPS (Im et al. 2003), the mean of unit-by-unit statistics (first-generation tests), applied to trace statistics instead of ADF t ratios, and it is asymptotically \(N(0, 1)\) (Larsson et al. 2001; Baltagi 2021, 361; Pesaran 2015, 849–50). It tests no cointegration in any unit against at most \(r_0 \ge 1\) relations, and unlike the residual tests it allows more than one relation per unit; the moments are tabulated for the model without deterministic terms by Larsson et al. (2001) and with a constant and trend by Breitung (2005; Pesaran 2015, 850). It needs a large T: with a short T the size is severely distorted however large N is (Baltagi 2021, 361).

title: Appendix I — Cointegration in panels
text:
I.5 Dependence
The unit-root note ends on the assumption no test checks: units may share a trend, and the traps step shows that no correlation statistic sees it. For cointegration tests the consequence is stated outright. The literature assumes one cointegrating vector per unit and lets units depend on each other only through short-run dynamics; when units are cointegrated with each other, “both univariate and multivariate panel cointegration tests can be substantially over-sized” (Banerjee et al. 2004; Baltagi 2021, 362). The remedy proposed is to extract each unit’s common trend by Johansen’s method and test for cointegration among the trends (Baltagi 2021, 362), a procedure demonstrated on panels of at most eight units (Pesaran 2015, 843).
A common factor is the gentler case, and it is enough to break the tests. Under the factor structure of Bai and Ng (2004), Kao’s and Pedroni’s statistics are no longer asymptotically normal and converge at the rate \(T\) rather than \(\sqrt N T\); the remedy is to estimate the factors, strip them from the data, and test the defactored residuals (Gengenbach et al. 2006; Baltagi 2021, 362). On the unit-root side, PANIC, the test that defactors by principal components and tests factors and remainders separately, is invalid in its pooled form: replacing the remainders by estimates biases the pooled statistic, and Bai and Ng (2010) supply an alternative (Westerlund and Larsson 2009; Pesaran 2015, 837). Pesaran’s verdict on the field is that “a general approach that is capable of addressing all the various issues involved does not exist if N is relatively large” (Pesaran 2015, 843).

title: Appendix I — Cointegration in panels
text:
I.6 Long-run estimation
Once the residual is stationary, the slope is the long-run elasticity, and the question is how to estimate it. OLS on a cointegrated panel is consistent at rate \(T\sqrt N\), so the years do more than the states, but with regressors that respond to the error it is inefficient (Pesaran 2015, 850). Two corrections share the field.
FMOLS adjusts the dependent variable for the part of the error that is correlated with the regressor’s innovations and subtracts a bias term from the cross product, both built from non-parametric long-run variances (Phillips and Moon 1999; Pedroni 2000; Pesaran 2015, 850–51, eqs. 31.51–31.52). DOLS does the same by regression: add leads and lags of \(\Delta x_{it}\) to the cointegrating regression, so that what is left is orthogonal to the regressor’s past and future (Kao and Chiang 2000; Pesaran 2015, 851, eqs. 31.53–31.54). The two have the same limiting distribution,
\[T\sqrt N\,(\hat\beta - \beta) \to
  N\!\left(0,\; 6\,\Omega_\varepsilon^{-1}
  \sigma^2_{u \mid \varepsilon}\right)\]
in the homogeneous case (Kao and Chiang 2000; Pesaran 2015, 851). Both maintain cross-sectional independence (Baltagi 2021, 364). Both also rest on kernel estimates of long-run variances, which perform poorly when T is under 20 (Pesaran 2015, 851). Breitung’s two-step estimator, which fits the short-run and long-run parameters separately, has a smaller small-sample bias and more reliable standard errors than either in his experiments (Breitung 2005; Pesaran 2015, 853); in the large simulation of Wagner and Hlouskova (2010), DOLS beats every other estimator, with FMOLS and the two-step estimator similar (Pesaran 2015, 853).
Under dependence. Three estimators relax independence, and all three represent it as a correlation between the units’ errors at the same date. DSUR is a GLS fit of the DOLS regression, OLS after reweighting by the long-run error covariance across units, for one homogeneous cointegrating vector (Mark et al. 2005; Moon and Perron 2005; Pesaran 2015, 853–54, eq. 31.57). Bai–Kao and Westerlund add stationary common factors to the error and run FMOLS around them; Bai–Kao–Ng allow non-stationary factors and estimate slope, factors and loadings by iterating on a least-squares criterion, with a bias correction (Bai and Kao 2006; Westerlund 2007a; Bai et al. 2009; Pesaran 2015, 854, eqs. 31.58–31.59). None of them allows cross-unit cointegration (Pesaran 2015, 854). The panel VECM that would, Johansen on the stacked vector, is the infeasible system of the precondition section (Groen and Kleibergen 2003; Pesaran 2015, 854–55, eq. 31.60).
The substitute the book runs. None of the above is in R. What is in R is CCE, the regression that adds cross-state averages of price and income to each state’s equation to stand in for the common factors (CCE). Its estimates are consistent whether the factors are stationary, non-stationary or cointegrated, so long as the idiosyncratic error is stationary and the number of factors fixed (Kapetanios et al. 2011; Pesaran 2015, 845). On these 49 states Holly et al. (2010) report CCEMG and CCEP slopes of 1.14 (0.20) and 1.20 (0.21), do not reject a unit elasticity, and test the gap \(p_{it} - y_{it}\) with CIPS, the panel unit-root test that defactors with the same averages (second-generation tests): statistics of −2.16 to −2.45 against a 5% value of −2.11, read as cointegration “for a sufficiently large number of States” (Pesaran 2015, 845–46). Croissant and Millo (2019, 209) shorten the route and run CIPS directly on the CCE residuals, with no deterministic term because the fit already carries one, and conclude that both CCE fits “represent cointegrating regressions”.
The book runs the second version and labels it a substitute, for two reasons. The CIPS critical values are those of a unit-root test on an observed series; the single-series literature shows that a residual has a distribution of its own, which is why Engle–Granger has its own tables (Pesaran 2015, 525). Holly et al. (2010) avoid the problem by fixing the slope at one before testing; the residual version does not. And CIPS tests the alternative that a share of units has a stationary residual (Pesaran 2007) (what a rejection means), so a rejection says that enough states’ gaps revert, not that every state’s does. What the substitute keeps is the one thing the estimators above lack: it allows the common shock that the CD test, the test of whether units move together, found in every state.

title: Appendix I — Cointegration in panels
text:
I.7 Finite samples
Two Monte Carlo studies set expectations for \(T = 29\). Gutierrez (2003) finds that at \(T = 10\) Kao’s tests have more power than Pedroni’s, and still little even at \(N = 100\); at large T Pedroni’s win; both beat the LR-bar. The danger runs both ways: with a long panel the whole panel is called cointegrated when a small fraction of units is, and with a short one it is called not cointegrated when a large fraction is (Gutierrez 2003; Baltagi 2021, 363). Wagner and Hlouskova (2010) cover the single-equation and the system tests at once. Two of Pedroni’s statistics, the ADF-based ones, perform best; every other test is severely undersized with low power, “dismal for \(T \le 25\)”; Pedroni’s are also the least affected by short-run dependence or cross-unit cointegration; and the system tests are very bad at small T and unreliable for the rank (Wagner and Hlouskova 2010; Baltagi 2021, 363; Pesaran 2015, 849).
The project’s own check, in the Pitfalls of the cointegration step, is of the implementation rather than the tests. At \(N = 49\), \(T = 29\), the five scale-free statistics as computed there reject in almost none of 200 draws without cointegration and in all 200 with it, and the other two change with the units of measurement, which Pedroni’s statistics cannot. They separate the hypotheses and fail the \(N(0, 1)\) calibration, so the step reports them as unverified.

title: Appendix I — Cointegration in panels
text:
I.8 If / then







If
Then




Both series fail to reject a unit root, state by state and as a panel
Test the residual before reading any slope: a pooled slope converges even with no cointegration (Phillips and Moon 1999; Baltagi 2021, 355).


A unit’s Johansen rank is 2
One of its series is stationary; the residual tests’ precondition \(r_i = 1\) fails there (Pesaran 2015, 839).


Johansen’s rank is read at \(T \approx 30\)
Report the tally, not the verdicts: the trace test is asymptotic and needs a reasonably large T (Pesaran 2015, 547).


The CD test rejects on the residuals
Kao, McCoskey–Kao and Pedroni lose their normal limits; defactor first (Gengenbach et al. 2006; Baltagi 2021, 362).


Units may share a trend
Every test above is over-sized; test the common trends for cointegration among themselves (Banerjee et al. 2004; Baltagi 2021, 362).


\(T \le 25\)
Expect low power from every residual test, and do not trust a system test’s rank (Wagner and Hlouskova 2010; Baltagi 2021, 363).


The slope is wanted and units are independent
DOLS, then FMOLS; both need T well above 20 for the long-run variances (Wagner and Hlouskova 2010; Pesaran 2015, 851, 853).


The slope is wanted and units share a factor
DSUR, Bai–Kao or Bai–Kao–Ng in principle; CCE with CIPS on its residual in this book, labelled a substitute (Pesaran 2015, 854; Croissant and Millo 2019, 209).


CIPS rejects on the CCE residual
A share of states’ price–income gaps revert; say “a share”, and say the critical values are those of a unit-root test (Pesaran 2015, 525).

title: Appendix I — Cointegration in panels
text:
I.9 Open

No implementation. Kao, McCoskey–Kao, Larsson–Lyhagen–Löthgren, Westerlund’s error-correction tests (Westerlund 2007b), FMOLS, DOLS, DSUR and the factor estimators have no R implementation in this project. The Stata benchmarks, xtcointtest kao, xtcointtest pedroni and xtcointtest westerlund, are deferred to a later plan.
pco. The only Pedroni implementation is archived on CRAN, two of its seven statistics depend on the units of measurement, and the moments it standardises with cannot be checked against Table 2 of Pedroni (1999), which is not in lit/. Its five remaining statistics are reported unverified.
The precondition at \(T = 29\). \(r_i = 1\) cannot be confirmed state by state; the tally of ranks is the evidence.
The substitute’s critical values. CIPS on a regression residual reads unit-root tables. No panel residual-based table exists for it, and this book does not simulate one.
Baltagi’s targets. Tables 12.3 to 12.7 of Baltagi (2021) run Kao, Pedroni, FMOLS and DOLS on the R&D panel of Kao et al. (1999), which ships in no R package. They are not reproduced.

title: Appendix I — Cointegration in panels
text:
I.10 Next
The long-run slope is settled by what the residual says. The next question is the error of an ordinary panel regression on stationary data, same slopes, same variance, no memory: the error of a panel regression. The road here began in panel unit roots.

title: Appendix J — Fixed and random effects
text:
J.1 Why the method exists
General Motors invests on a scale Westinghouse never reaches, at the same market value and the same capital stock. Each of Grunfeld’s ten firms (Grunfeld 1958) has a character of its own, and so does each of the 49 states whose house prices run through this book. Call that character \(\alpha_i\), the unit effect: everything about unit i that does not change over the sample and is not in the regression. In an earnings equation it is unobserved ability; in a production function it is managerial skill (Baltagi 2021, 15).
One pooled regression puts \(\alpha_i\) in the error, and that does two kinds of damage. The errors of one unit are then correlated across every pair of years by the same amount, so the pooled standard errors are wrong (Moulton 1986; Baltagi 2021, 24, 54). And if \(\alpha_i\) moves with the regressors, as ability moves with schooling, the pooled slope is biased: an omitted-variable bias, since the unit dummies that belong in the equation were left out (Baltagi 2021, 18).
Fixed effects treat \(\alpha_i\) as a parameter, one per unit, and either estimate it with a dummy or wipe it out by taking each unit’s data in deviation from its own mean. The price is that only within-unit variation is left: \(N - 1\) degrees of freedom are gone, and any regressor that does not change over time, sex, schooling, a state’s land area, is wiped out with the effect (Baltagi 2021, 17). Random effects treat \(\alpha_i\) as a draw, \(\alpha_i \sim \mathrm{IID}(0, \sigma^2_\alpha)\), independent of the regressors. The price is that independence assumption; the gain is efficiency, because between-unit variation is used too, and a coefficient on the time-invariant regressors (Baltagi 2021, 17, 24, 27). Mundlak put the choice sharply: random effects assume every regressor is uncorrelated with \(\alpha_i\), fixed effects allow every one to be correlated, “an ‘all’ or ‘nothing’ choice” (Mundlak 1978; Baltagi 2021, 28). The rest of this note is about how to tell whether \(\alpha_i\) is there at all, and then which of the two stories fits.

title: Appendix J — Fixed and random effects
text:
J.2 1. One error, two components
One regression for all units assumes two things: the same slopes for every unit, and an error whose only structure is the unit effect. Write the model as
\[
y_{it} = \beta' x_{it} + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad
u_{it} = \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it},
\]
with \(\varepsilon_{it} \sim \mathrm{IID}(0, \sigma^2_\varepsilon)\), the one-way error component model (Baltagi 2021, eqs. 2.1–2.2, p. 15). The two-way model adds a time effect, \(u_{it} = \alpha_i + \delta_t +
\varepsilon_{it}\), a strike year or an oil shock that hits every unit in that year (Baltagi 2021, eq. 3.1, p. 47); Baltagi writes it \(\lambda_t\). The same-slopes assumption is poolability, and its tests, Chow’s F, Roy–Zellner and Swamy’s random coefficients (Chow 1960; Roy 1957; Zellner 1962; Swamy 1970), are in the error note; this note takes the slopes as common and asks what \(\alpha_i\) is.
Under random effects the composite error has covariance
\[
\Omega = \sigma^2_\alpha (I_N \otimes J_T) + \sigma^2_\varepsilon I_{NT},
\]
where \(J_T\) is a \(T \times T\) matrix of ones (Baltagi 2021, eq. 2.17, p. 24). Two errors of the same unit, any two years apart, are correlated by \(\rho = \sigma^2_\alpha / (\sigma^2_\alpha + \sigma^2_\varepsilon)\), however far apart the years; errors of different units are uncorrelated (Baltagi 2021, 24). That constant \(\rho\) is the signature of a unit effect, and the serial-correlation tests of the error note are built to tell it from an autoregressive error, whose correlation dies out with the distance between years.

title: Appendix J — Fixed and random effects
text:
J.3 2. Within, between and GLS
Two projection matrices do all the work. \(P = I_N \otimes \bar J_T\), with \(\bar J_T = J_T / T\), replaces every observation by its unit mean; \(Q =
I_{NT} - P\) takes deviations from the unit mean. They are symmetric, idempotent, orthogonal, and sum to the identity (Baltagi 2021, 16; Croissant and Millo 2019, 25). The within estimator regresses \(Qy\) on \(QX\),
\[
\hat\beta_W = (X'QX)^{-1} X'Qy,
\]
and \(Q\) wipes out \(\alpha_i\) with the unit means (Baltagi 2021, eq. 2.7, p. 17). The between estimator regresses the unit means on each other, \(\hat\beta_B = (X'PX)^{-1} X'Py\), and uses only the variation across units (Baltagi 2021, eq. 2.25, p. 26). Pooled OLS weights the two sources of variation equally; GLS weights them by the inverse of their variances (Baltagi 2021, 26–27). With \(\phi^2 = \sigma^2_\varepsilon /
\sigma^2_1\) and \(\sigma^2_1 = T\sigma^2_\alpha + \sigma^2_\varepsilon\),
\[
\hat\beta_{GLS} = W_1 \hat\beta_W + W_2 \hat\beta_B, \qquad
W_1 = [X'QX + \phi^2 X'PX]^{-1} X'QX, \quad W_2 = I - W_1,
\]
a matrix-weighted average of within and between (Baltagi 2021, eq. 2.31, pp. 26–27; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 2.4.1, p. 39). Two limits say what the estimator is doing. If \(\sigma^2_\alpha = 0\) then \(\phi^2 = 1\) and GLS is OLS. If \(T \to \infty\) then \(\phi^2 \to 0\) and GLS is within (Baltagi 2021, 27; Pesaran 2015, 653): with enough years per unit the two stories give the same slope, and the fixed-or-random question only bites when T is short.
In practice GLS is OLS on quasi-demeaned data. Premultiplying by \(\Omega^{-1/2}\) turns \(y_{it}\) into \(y_{it} - \theta \bar y_{i\cdot}\) with
\[
\theta = 1 - \frac{\sigma_\varepsilon}{\sigma_1}
  = 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + T\sigma^2_\alpha / \sigma^2_\varepsilon}},
\]
the fraction of the unit mean that is removed (Baltagi 2021, eq. 2.20, p. 25; Croissant and Millo 2019, 35). \(\theta = 0\) is pooled OLS, \(\theta = 1\) is within, and plm::ercomp prints it: 0.86 on Grunfeld, which is why every feasible GLS fit there sits next to the within fit (Baltagi 2021, 31).
The variance components have to be estimated first, and the menu in random.method is a menu of residuals. Wallace–Hussain use pooled OLS residuals in the two quadratic forms \(u'Pu/N\) and \(u'Qu/N(T-1)\) (Wallace and Hussain 1969); Amemiya uses the within residuals instead, which gives the same asymptotic distribution as knowing the true disturbances (Amemiya 1971; Baltagi 2021, eqs. 2.21–2.23, p. 25); Swamy–Arora take \(\hat\sigma^2_\varepsilon\) from the within regression’s mean square and \(\hat\sigma^2_1\) from the between regression’s (Swamy and Arora 1972; Baltagi 2021, eqs. 2.24 and 2.27, pp. 25–26); Nerlove estimates \(\sigma^2_\alpha\) as the sample variance of the estimated dummies (Nerlove 1971; Baltagi 2021, 27; Croissant and Millo 2019, 36–37). All but Nerlove recover \(\sigma^2_\alpha = (\sigma^2_1 - \sigma^2_\varepsilon)/T\) by subtraction, and nothing stops the difference from being negative. In the one-way model the fix is to set it to zero, which happens only when the true variance is near zero, when OLS is fine anyway, so “replacing negative \(\sigma^2_\mu\) by zero is not a sin after all” (Baltagi 2021, 27). In the two-way model Baltagi’s Monte Carlo says the opposite: a negative estimate cannot be told from a misspecified model, and “the researcher should not label the problem of negative variance estimates ‘not serious’” (Baltagi 1981; 2021, 56).
The two-way model has four distinct roots of \(\Omega\) and three variance components, so GLS is a matrix-weighted average of three estimators: within, between units \(\hat\beta_B\) and between periods \(\hat\beta_C\) (Baltagi 2021, eqs. 3.13 and 3.24, pp. 51–53), and Swamy–Arora’s recipe needs three regressions (Baltagi 2021, eqs. 3.19–3.21, p. 52). The time variance component is estimated from \(T - 1\) period means, so on a panel with 20 years it is the one most likely to come back negative. That is what happens to Grunfeld under Swamy–Arora and Wallace–Hussain (Baltagi 2021, 99), and it is why the two-way Hausman statistic of section 5 depends on the method.

title: Appendix J — Fixed and random effects
section: J.4 3. Is there an effect at all
text:
J.4 3. Is there an effect at all
The Breusch–Pagan test asks whether pooled OLS residuals from one unit resemble each other more than chance allows. It is a Lagrange multiplier test: a score test that needs only the restricted model, here pooled OLS, and under normality the score for \(\sigma^2_\alpha\) is a function of the ratio of the summed squared unit totals to the summed squared residuals (Breusch and Pagan 1980; Baltagi 2021, eqs. 4.17–4.22, pp. 81–82). For \(H_0: \sigma^2_\alpha = 0\),
\[
LM_1 = \frac{NT}{2(T-1)}
  \left[ \frac{\hat u'(I_N \otimes J_T)\hat u}{\hat u'\hat u} - 1 \right]^2
  \;\sim\; \chi^2_1 ,
\]
and the test of \(\sigma^2_\delta = 0\) swaps \(I_N \otimes J_T\) for \(J_N
\otimes I_T\) and \(T - 1\) for \(N - 1\); the two-way test of both is their sum, \(\chi^2_2\) (Baltagi 2021, eqs. 4.22–4.24, p. 82).
The alternative of a two-sided test is “the variance is not zero”, and a variance cannot be negative. Honda takes the signed square root,
\[
A = \sqrt{\frac{NT}{2(T-1)}}
  \left[ \frac{\hat u'(I_N \otimes J_T)\hat u}{\hat u'\hat u} - 1 \right]
  \;\sim\; N(0, 1),
\]
and rejects only for large positive values; it is uniformly most powerful for the one-sided alternative and robust to non-normality (Honda 1985; Baltagi 2021, eq. 4.25, p. 83). The sign matters. On Grunfeld the time-effect statistic is \(B = -2.540\): the one-sided test does not reject, but \(B^2 =
6.454\) is above the \(\chi^2_1\) critical value 3.841 and the two-sided test does. The one-sided test is right; “these data clearly support the use of the one-sided test in empirical applications” (Baltagi 2021, 87).
For both effects at once Honda offers the “handy” \((A + B)/\sqrt 2\), which is \(N(0, 1)\) under the null (Baltagi 2021, 83). King–Wu replace the equal weights by the locally mean most powerful ones,
\[
KW = \sqrt{\frac{T-1}{N+T-2}}\, A + \sqrt{\frac{N-1}{N+T-2}}\, B ,
\]
also \(N(0, 1)\) (King and Wu 1997; Baltagi et al. 1992; Baltagi 2021, eq. 4.30, p. 84). Both can be dragged down by a negative piece. Gourieroux, Holly and Monfort drop a negative piece instead of adding it:
\[
\chi^2_m =
\begin{cases}
A^2 + B^2 & A > 0,\ B > 0 \\
A^2       & A > 0,\ B \le 0 \\
B^2       & A \le 0,\ B > 0 \\
0         & A \le 0,\ B \le 0 ,
\end{cases}
\qquad
\chi^2_m \sim \tfrac14 \chi^2(0) + \tfrac12 \chi^2(1) + \tfrac14 \chi^2(2),
\]
a mixed chi-square whose weights come from A and B being asymptotically independent; it “is immune to the possible negative values of A and B” (Gourieroux et al. 1982; Baltagi et al. 1992; Baltagi 2021, eq. 4.33, p. 84). In Baltagi, Chang and Li’s Monte Carlo, Breusch–Pagan, Honda and King–Wu all under-size the joint test when a piece is negative, while GHM and the F test hold their size (Baltagi et al. 1992; Baltagi 2021, 86). plm::plmtest(type = "ghm") exists for effect = "twoways" only, which is where it is needed.
Two refinements are not implemented. Moulton and Randolph showed that the \(N(0, 1)\) approximation for Honda’s statistic “can be poor even in large samples … when the number of regressors is large or the intra-class correlation of some of the regressors is high”, and proposed the standardized LM test, Honda’s statistic centred and scaled by the exact mean and variance of the quadratic form, \(SLM = (d - E(d))/\sqrt{\mathrm{var}(d)}\) with \(d = \hat u' D \hat u / \hat u'\hat u\) (Moulton and Randolph 1989; Honda 1991; Baltagi 2021, eqs. 4.26–4.28 and 4.31, pp. 83–84). Spatially smooth regressors have a high intra-class correlation, so this is the case of this book. And testing \(\sigma^2_\alpha = 0\) with Honda’s statistic “implicitly assumes that the time-specific effects do not exist”, which “may lead to incorrect decisions especially when the variance of the time effects (assumed to be zero) is large”. The conditional LM tests of Baltagi, Chang and Li test one variance allowing the other to be positive, from one-way GLS residuals (Baltagi et al. 1992; Baltagi 2021, eqs. 4.34 and 4.36, p. 85); the Monte Carlo verdict is that “one should not ignore the possibility that \(\sigma^2_\lambda > 0\) when testing \(\sigma^2_\mu = 0\)”, and that over-specifying the model as two-way costs little (Baltagi 2021, 86). plmtest(effect = "twoways") tests both variances jointly; it is not this conditional test.
The oldest test is an F on the unit dummies: pooled OLS is the restricted model, within the unrestricted, and
\[
F = \frac{(RRSS - URSS)/(N-1)}{URSS/(NT - N - K)}
  \;\sim\; F_{N-1,\, N(T-1)-K}
\]
[Baltagi (2021), eq. 2.12, p. 18; eq. 4.38, p. 85]. In the two-way model there are three such tests: both sets of dummies against pooled OLS, unit dummies given time dummies, and time dummies given unit dummies, each with the two-way within fit as the unrestricted model (Baltagi 2021, eqs. 3.8–3.9, p. 49). These conditional F tests are exact in finite samples under normality (Baltagi 2021, 85), “perform reasonably well when compared to the LR and LM tests, for both the one-way and two-way models and are recommended” (Baltagi 2021, 87); they are the three rows of Baltagi’s Table 4.3 (Baltagi 2021, 89), and plm::pFtest on two nested within fits is the conditional pair.

title: Appendix J — Fixed and random effects
section: J.5 4. Fixed or random: the Hausman contrast
text:
J.5 4. Fixed or random: the Hausman contrast
Everything above finds an effect; nothing says whether it is correlated with the regressors. The random-effects GLS estimator is efficient when \(E(u_{it} \mid X_{it}) = 0\) and inconsistent otherwise; the within estimator is consistent either way, because \(Q\) removed \(\alpha_i\) before the regression. Hausman’s idea is to compare them: if both are consistent they should agree, and the covariance of an efficient estimator with its difference from any other consistent estimator is zero, so the variance of the difference is the difference of the variances (Hausman 1978; Baltagi 2021, 89–90; Pesaran 2015, eq. 26.52, p. 660). With \(\hat q_1 =
\hat\beta_{GLS} - \hat\beta_W\),
\[
\mathrm{var}(\hat q_1)
  = \mathrm{var}(\hat\beta_W) - \mathrm{var}(\hat\beta_{GLS}),
\qquad
m_1 = \hat q_1' [\mathrm{var}(\hat q_1)]^{-1} \hat q_1 \;\sim\; \chi^2_K
\]
(Baltagi 2021, eqs. 4.40–4.41, p. 90). The same test is a Wald test in an augmented regression: quasi-demean \(y\) and \(X\) as GLS does, add the within-demeaned regressors \(\tilde X = QX\), and test their coefficient,
\[
y^* = X^*\beta + \tilde X \gamma + w, \qquad H_0: \gamma = 0
\]
(Baltagi 2021, eq. 4.42, p. 90). OLS on this regression returns \(\hat\beta = \hat\beta_B\) and \(\hat\gamma = \hat\beta_W - \hat\beta_B\), with \(\mathrm{var}(\hat\gamma) = \mathrm{var}(\hat\beta_W) +
\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta_B)\), a sum, since the two use orthogonal pieces of the data (Baltagi 2021, eqs. 4.46–4.48, pp. 90–91). Hausman and Taylor proved that the three contrasts, GLS against within, GLS against between, and within against between, give numerically identical statistics (Hausman and Taylor 1981; Baltagi 2021, 91); phtest(method = "chisq") is \(m_1\) and method = "aux" is the augmented regression. On Grunfeld they are 2.33 and 2.13, the difference being only which \(\hat\sigma^2_\varepsilon\) enters the variance (Baltagi 2021, 95).
The augmented regression is also how the test is made robust. Under heteroskedasticity or serial correlation neither estimator is efficient, so the variance of the contrast is no longer a difference of variances and \(m_1\) is wrong. Arellano writes the contrast as a regression on forward orthogonal deviations stacked over unit means, with \(\hat\gamma =
\hat\beta_B - \hat\beta_W\), and tests \(\gamma = 0\) with White’s robust covariance (Arellano 1993; Baltagi 2021, eq. 4.49, pp. 91–92); “a simpler robust Hausman test can be obtained by testing for \(\gamma = 0\) from the artificial regression (4.42) using the robust variance-covariance matrix option” (Baltagi 2021, 92; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 5.1.3.1, p. 125), which is phtest(method = "aux", vcov = plm::vcovHC). On Grunfeld Baltagi’s robust F(2, 195) is 1.58, p 0.208 (Baltagi 2021, 95); with ten clusters the Arellano covariance is itself noisy, since the estimator is asymptotic in the number of clusters (Croissant and Millo 2019, 110), and the step reports what plm gives.
Mundlak’s reading says what is being tested. Let the unit effect be a linear function of the unit means of the regressors,
\[
\alpha_i = \pi' \bar x_{i\cdot} + w_i, \qquad
w_i \sim \mathrm{IID}(0, \sigma^2_w).
\]
Substituting it in gives \(y = X\beta + PX\pi + (w + \varepsilon)\), with \(w\) the \(w_i\) stacked over the \(NT\) observations, an error-components model with the unit means as extra regressors. GLS on it returns \(\hat\beta =
\hat\beta_W\) and \(\hat\pi = \hat\beta_B - \hat\beta_W\): once the correlation is modelled, the efficient estimator is within, and the random-effects estimator is biased because it ignores \(\pi\) (Mundlak 1978; Baltagi 2021, eqs. 7.33–7.38, pp. 170–171; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 4.2.1, pp. 89–90). Hausman’s test is the test of \(\pi = 0\). It is worth saying what a rejection does not show. “Rejecting the null of the Hausman test implies that the RE estimator is not consistent. This does not necessarily mean that the FE restrictions are satisfied” (Baltagi 2021, 93). Chamberlain’s restrictions, that the reduced-form regression of each year’s \(y\) on every year’s \(x\) has the structure \(\Pi = (I_T \otimes \beta') +
\iota_T \lambda'\), are testable; Angrist and Newey showed that the minimum chi-square statistic is a sum over periods of degrees of freedom times the \(R^2\) from regressing that period’s within residuals on all leads and lags of the regressors (Chamberlain 1982; Angrist and Newey 1991; Baltagi 2021, eqs. 4.50–4.53, pp. 92–93; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 4.2.3, pp. 90–93). Both need N large against \(TK\): the statistic has \((T^2 - T - 1)K\) degrees of freedom (Croissant and Millo 2019, 93), and the minimum chi-square test understates its variance as T grows (Baltagi 2021, 93). plm::piest fails on ten firms and on the 595 workers; aneweytest runs on the workers, and both run on the 171 rice farms. One more caution: using the Hausman test to pick the estimator and then testing \(\beta\) distorts the size of the second test, and Guggenberger’s advice is fixed-effects inference without the pretest (Guggenberger 2010; Baltagi 2021, 94).

title: Appendix J — Fixed and random effects
Appendix J — Fixed and random effects
text:
J.7 6. Time-invariant regressors
A rejection sends the reader to fixed effects, and fixed effects cannot estimate the return to schooling, because schooling does not change over the seven years of the wage panel. Hausman and Taylor keep some of the random-effects story. Split the regressors into \(X = [X_1, X_2]\) and the time-invariant ones into \(Z = [Z_1, Z_2]\), where the “1” blocks are uncorrelated with \(\alpha_i\) and the “2” blocks are correlated with it but not with \(\varepsilon_{it}\):
\[
y_{it} = \beta' x_{it} + \gamma' z_i + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it}
\]
(Hausman and Taylor 1981; Baltagi 2021, eq. 7.40, p. 171; Pesaran 2015, sec. 26.10, p. 665). The within transformation sweeps \(\alpha_i\) and \(z_i\) together. The HT estimator is instead 2SLS on the \(\Omega^{-1/2}\)-transformed model with instruments the panel generates itself, \(A_{HT} = [QX_1, QX_2, PX_1, Z_1]\): deviations of every time-varying regressor, which are orthogonal to \(\alpha_i\) by construction, plus the unit means of the exogenous ones and the exogenous time-invariant regressors (Baltagi 2021, 171; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 6.3.2.3, p. 146). \(X_1\) is used twice, as means and as deviations, so the order condition is \(k_1 \ge g_2\): at least as many exogenous time-varying regressors as endogenous time-invariant ones (Baltagi 2021, 171; Croissant and Millo 2019, 146). If \(k_1 = g_2\) the slopes on \(X\) are the within slopes; if \(k_1 > g_2\) the model is over-identified, HT is more efficient than within, and a Hausman contrast of the two tests the over-identifying restrictions, \(\chi^2\) with \(k_1 - g_2\) degrees of freedom (Baltagi 2021, eq. 7.46, p. 172). On the wage panel Baltagi reads \(\chi^2_3
= 5.26\) as not rejecting, with three degrees of freedom “since there are three over-identifying conditions” (Baltagi 2021, 175); plm::phtest reports the number of common coefficients instead, nine, and the step says so.
Amemiya and MaCurdy add \(X_1\) at every period as instruments, which needs \(X_1\) to be uncorrelated with \(\alpha_i\) period by period and not only on average (Amemiya and MaCurdy 1986; Baltagi 2021, 173; Croissant and Millo 2019, 147); Breusch, Mizon and Schmidt add the deviations of \(X_2\) at every period too (Breusch et al. 1989; Baltagi 2021, 173). Each set nests the one before, so the extra assumptions are testable by a Hausman contrast of the two fits (Croissant and Millo 2019, 147), and the Cornwell–Rupert replication is the book’s worked case: GLS puts the return to schooling at 10 %, HT at 13.8 %, and the HT-versus-AM contrast does not reject (Cornwell and Rupert 1988; Baltagi and Khanti-Akom 1990; Baltagi 2021, 174–76). When \(z_i\) is uncorrelated with \(\alpha_i\) no instrument is needed: regress the unit means of the within residuals on \(z_i\) (Pesaran 2015, sec. 26.10.1, pp. 663–664).

text:
J.8 If / then







If
Then




Honda’s statistic is negative
No effect of that kind; do not read the squared Breusch–Pagan value as a rejection (Baltagi 2021, 87)


Both effects are in question
Read GHM or the conditional F tests, which hold their size when a piece is negative (Baltagi 2021, 86–87)


Regressors are many or spatially smooth
Honda’s \(N(0, 1)\) reference can be poor; the SLM correction is not implemented (Baltagi 2021, 83)


An effect is found and Hausman does not reject
Random effects is admissible and more efficient; report it beside within (Baltagi 2021, 90)


Hausman rejects
Random effects is inconsistent; fixed effects is not thereby validated, and the Chamberlain restrictions remain to be tested (Baltagi 2021, 93)


Errors are heteroskedastic or serially correlated
The \(\chi^2\) form is wrong; use the augmented regression with a robust covariance (Baltagi 2021, 92)


T is long
GLS and within converge; the choice matters little (Baltagi 2021, 27; Pesaran 2015, 653)


The two-way time variance comes back negative
The two-way Hausman statistic depends on the variance method; check whether a time effect is there at all (Baltagi 2021, 56, 99–101)


A time-invariant regressor matters and is endogenous
Hausman–Taylor with \(k_1 \ge g_2\); test the instruments against within (Baltagi 2021, 171–72)

title: Appendix J — Fixed and random effects
text:
J.9 Open

The standardized LM tests of Moulton–Randolph and Honda, Baltagi’s eq. 4.26, are not implemented: plmtest has no type = "slm", and the “Standardized” rows of Baltagi’s Table 4.2 cannot be reproduced (Baltagi 2021, 83, 88).
The conditional LM tests of Baltagi, Chang and Li, eqs. 4.34 and 4.36, are not implemented; plmtest(effect = "twoways") is the joint test (Baltagi 2021, 85).
Kang’s five hypotheses have one implementation, hypothesis 5; phtest(effect = "time") compares one-way time fixed with one-way time random effects and is none of Baltagi’s Table 4.6 (Baltagi 2021, 99–100).
Wansbeek–Kapteyn variance components are not a random.method, so Baltagi’s two-way 8.842 is not reproduced (Baltagi 2021, 99).
Chamberlain’s and Angrist–Newey’s tests need \(N \gg TK\), with \((T^2 - T - 1)K\) restrictions to test (Croissant and Millo 2019, 93; Baltagi 2021, 93); piest fails on Grunfeld and on the wage panel, and the chapter reproduces both tests on the rice farms.

title: Appendix K — The error of a panel regression
text:
K.1 Why one regression can lie
One investment equation for ten firms, one price–income elasticity for 49 states: a pooled regression makes three promises about its error. The slopes are the same for every unit, so that what is left over is noise and not a different line. The noise has the same variance everywhere, so that General Motors’ shocks are no wilder than Diamond Match’s. And the noise has no memory, so that this year’s shock says nothing about next year’s beyond what the unit effect already says. Each promise can be broken, each break has a test, and each test has a repair.
The repairs are not the same kind. A wrong slope is a bias, and only a different estimator fixes it. Unequal variances and memory leave the slopes consistent and make the standard errors wrong, in either direction (Baltagi 2021, 109, 115), so the first repair is an honest standard error, and the second, when the structure is known well enough, is an estimator that reweights the data and recovers efficiency. This note takes the three promises in turn and ends with the menu of standard errors.
crumbs: K  The error of a panel regression

title: Appendix K — The error of a panel regression
section: K.2 1. The composite error and its memory
text:
K.2 1. The composite error and its memory
Write the error of a one-way panel regression as \(u_{it} = \alpha_i +
\varepsilon_{it}\), where \(\alpha_i\) is the unit effect, everything fixed about unit i that the regression leaves out, and \(\varepsilon_{it}\) is the remainder, the shock of unit i in year t (fixed and random effects). Under random effects the covariance is \(\Omega = \sigma^2_\alpha (I_N \otimes J_T) + \sigma^2_\varepsilon I_{NT}\), so two errors of the same unit are correlated by \(\sigma^2_\alpha /
(\sigma^2_\alpha + \sigma^2_\varepsilon)\) whatever the gap between the years (Baltagi 2021, eq. 2.17, p. 24). A unit effect is therefore “serial correlation that does not die out over time”, and any test for serial correlation run on pooled residuals will find it (Croissant and Millo 2019, 95).
Memory of the other kind decays. Let the remainder follow a first-order autoregression, an AR(1),
\[
\varepsilon_{it} = \rho\, \varepsilon_{i,t-1} + \eta_{it}, \qquad |\rho| < 1,
\quad \eta_{it} \sim \mathrm{IID}(0, \sigma^2_\eta),
\]
so that a shock to investment this year carries into the next few years and fades (Baltagi 2021, eq. 5.8, p. 115). The covariance of a unit’s errors is then
\[
E(u_i u_i') = \sigma^2_\alpha J_T + \sigma^2_\varepsilon V_\rho, \qquad
V_\rho = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & \rho & \cdots & \rho^{T-1} \\
\rho & 1 & \cdots & \rho^{T-2} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\rho^{T-1} & \rho^{T-2} & \cdots & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\]
a constant floor from \(\alpha_i\) plus a band that thins with the distance between years: the AR(1) counterpart, on p. 126, of Baltagi’s eq. 5.32, which is written for an MA(1) remainder, a shock that lingers one period (Baltagi 2021, 125–26). The tests of section 4 are all ways of telling the floor from the band. The limit of the band is a unit root in the error, \(\rho = 1\), a shock that never fades (why unit roots matter); that case is the boundary this chapter hands to dynamic panels.
Two transformations of the chapter leave their own fingerprint, and the tests have to know it. Taking each unit’s data in deviation from its mean, the within transformation, turns uncorrelated remainders into residuals with correlation \(-1/(T-1)\) between any two years; first differencing turns them into residuals with correlation \(-0.5\) between neighbours and zero beyond (Wooldridge 2010; Croissant and Millo 2019, 101, 103). A test of “no serial correlation” on within residuals is therefore a test against \(-1/(T-1)\), not against zero.
crumbs: K  The error of a panel regression

title: Appendix K — The error of a panel regression
text:
K.3 2. Same slopes
Chow’s F fits one regression to everyone and one to each unit and compares residual sums of squares. With \(N\) units, \(K' = K + 1\) coefficients each, the restricted residual sum \(e'e\) and the unrestricted one \(\sum_i e_i'e_i\),
\[
F = \frac{(e'e - \sum_i e_i'e_i)/(N-1)K'}{\sum_i e_i'e_i / N(T-K')}
  \;\sim\; F_{(N-1)K',\, N(T-K')}
\]
under \(H_0: \beta_i = \beta\) for all i and spherical errors, \(u \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I_{NT})\) (Chow 1960; Baltagi 2021, eq. 4.8, p. 77). Restricting the slopes only, with the within fit as the restricted model, gives the same statistic on \((N-1)K\) and \(N(T-K-1)\) degrees of freedom (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 8.2.3, p. 192). Pooling across years instead of units swaps the roles of N and T.
Spherical errors is the catch. Under a random unit effect the Chow F “is not the right test to perform”: transform the model by \(\Omega^{-1/2}\) first, so that the errors become spherical, then run the Chow F on the transformed data. That is the Roy–Zellner test, operational once \(\Omega\) is replaced by a consistent estimate (Roy 1957; Zellner 1962; Baltagi 2021, eqs. 4.9–4.14, pp. 77–79). Baltagi’s Monte Carlo on a two-way model with poolable data found the plain Chow test rejecting the true null with “a high frequency” whenever the variance components were not small, and the Roy–Zellner test holding its size (Baltagi 1981; 2021, 79). On Grunfeld the two tests agree, 27.75 and 4.35 on F(27, 170), both rejections (Baltagi 2021, 80); the point is the size, not the verdict. And a rejection is a statement about bias, not about what to report: “imposing the pooling restriction reduces the variance of the pooled estimator but may introduce bias if these restrictions are false” (Croissant and Millo 2019, 186), which is why the chapter shows the spread of the individual slopes beside the pooled one.
Swamy’s random coefficients make the spread a parameter. Let each unit’s coefficient vector be a draw around a common mean,
\[
y_i = Z_i \beta_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
\beta_i = \beta + \eta_i, \quad \eta_i \sim (0, \Delta),
\]
so that the error of unit i becomes \(\varepsilon_i + Z_i \eta_i\) with covariance \(\sigma^2_i I_T + Z_i \Delta Z_i'\): heteroskedastic across units and correlated within them (Swamy 1970; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 8.2.2, p. 187). Swamy’s estimator of the spread subtracts the sampling noise of the unit-by-unit OLS slopes from their empirical covariance,
\[
\hat\Delta = \frac{1}{N-1}
  \sum_i (\hat\beta_i - \bar\beta)(\hat\beta_i - \bar\beta)'
  - \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \hat\sigma^2_i (Z_i'Z_i)^{-1},
\]
and GLS with the implied covariance is the Swamy estimator of \(\beta\) (Croissant and Millo 2019, 188). The subtraction can leave \(\hat\Delta\) not positive definite. The mean-group estimator, the plain average of the unit slopes with the empirical covariance of the \(\hat\beta_i\) as its dispersion (common correlated effects), is Swamy’s with equal weights, “always non-negative definite”, and the two converge as T grows (Croissant and Millo 2019, 190). plm::pvcm(model = "random") returns \(\hat\Delta\) in $Delta.
Swamy also gave a test of \(\beta_i = \beta\): the weighted dispersion of the unit slopes around the pooled estimator,
\[
\hat S = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (\hat\beta_i - \hat\beta_{WFE})'
  \frac{X_i' M_\tau X_i}{\hat\sigma^2_i} (\hat\beta_i - \hat\beta_{WFE}),
\]
which is \(\chi^2_{k(N-1)}\) as \(T \to \infty\) with N fixed; it was built for panels “where N is small relative to T” (Swamy 1970; Pesaran 2015, eq. 28.78, pp. 737–738). With 49 states and 29 years, or 10 firms and 20, the fixed-N asymptotics are not the ones at hand. Pesaran and Yamagata standardise the same dispersion so that it is normal as N and T both grow,
\[
\hat\Delta = \sqrt N \, \frac{N^{-1}\hat S - k}{\sqrt{2k}}, \qquad
\tilde\Delta = \sqrt N \, \frac{N^{-1}\tilde S - k}{\sqrt{2k}},
\]
where \(\tilde S\) replaces each \(\hat\sigma^2_i\) by a variance computed from the pooled fixed-effects residuals. Both tend to \(N(0, 1)\) under the null, \(\hat\Delta\) if \(\sqrt N / T \to 0\) and \(\tilde\Delta\) under the weaker \(\sqrt N / T^2 \to 0\); under normal errors the mean-and-variance adjusted versions are valid with no restriction on how N and T grow (Pesaran and Yamagata 2008; Pesaran 2015, eq. 28.79, pp. 738–739). The price is in the assumptions: errors independent across units and years and homoskedastic within a unit, regressors strictly exogenous (Pesaran 2015, 739). Every other section of this note is about panels that break at least one, which is why Blomquist and Westerlund’s heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation robust version exists (Blomquist and Westerlund 2013). Neither test is implemented in R; Stata’s xthst is the reference implementation (Bersvendsen and Ditzen 2021), and the chapter states this as a limitation. A Hausman-type contrast of the fixed-effects and mean-group slopes is the other candidate, and it lacks power in every direction when the slopes are random draws, which is exactly Swamy’s alternative (Pesaran and Yamagata 2008; Baltagi 2021, 101).

title: Appendix K — The error of a panel regression
text:
K.4 3. Same variance
Big units have big shocks. Heteroskedasticity, unequal error variances, is the rule “where the cross-sectional units may be of varying size”, and it leaves the slopes consistent but not efficient while the classical standard errors “will be biased” (Baltagi 2021, 109). In a panel it can sit in either component: Mazodier and Trognon put it in the unit effect, \(\alpha_i \sim (0, w_i^2)\), which gives each unit its own quasi-demeaning fraction \(\theta_i\) (Mazodier and Trognon 1978); the alternative puts it in the remainder, \(\varepsilon_{it} \sim (0, w_i^2)\); and “it is hard to claim that it is in one component and not the other” (Baltagi 2021, eqs. 5.1–5.7, pp. 109–111).
The tests are the gap. Verbon’s Lagrange multiplier test takes both variances to be the same parametric function of time-invariant unit characteristics \(Z_i\) (Verbon 1980; Baltagi 2021, 113). Lejeune’s tests let \(\sigma^2_{\varepsilon,it}\) and \(\sigma^2_{\alpha,i}\) be distinct functions of exogenous variables and test homoskedasticity jointly with the absence of unit effects, so that OLS is the restricted model, once for a random and once for a fixed effect (Lejeune 2006; Baltagi 2021, 113–14). Neither has an R implementation, and no panel test of homoskedasticity does; the chapter shows the fan of residual spread against unit size and runs a cross-section test on the within-transformed data as a substitute, labelled as one.
The repair that needs no test is Arellano’s variance for the within estimator. Stack each unit’s \(T\) within-transformed observations, allow any \(T \times T\) covariance \(\Sigma_i\) inside a unit and none across units, and estimate the middle of White’s sandwich with the unit’s own residual outer product:
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{var}}(\hat\beta_W) = (\tilde X'\tilde X)^{-1}
  \Big[ \sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde X_i' \tilde u_i \tilde u_i' \tilde X_i \Big]
  (\tilde X'\tilde X)^{-1}
\]
(Arellano 1987; White 1980; Baltagi 2021, eqs. 2.13–2.16, pp. 18–19). It is robust to heteroskedasticity and to serial correlation of any form within a unit, and its asymptotics are \(N \to \infty\) with T fixed (Baltagi 2021, 18). The plain White estimator on the within fit, which allows only the variances to differ, is inconsistent for fixed T (Baltagi 2021, 19), and it understates the problem on every panel in the chapter. When T is large as well, consistency needs either a limit on the serial correlation or \(T/N \to 0\) (Pesaran 2015, sec. 26.7, p. 655).
The repair that recovers efficiency is feasible GLS on the whole \(T
\times T\) block. Assume \(\Omega = I_N \otimes \Sigma_T\) with \(\Sigma_T\) unrestricted but the same for every unit, estimate it from the cross-section,
\[
\hat\Sigma_T = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \hat e_i \hat e_i',
\]
and run GLS with it: the general GLS of Wooldridge, also called the Parks estimator, a variant of Zellner’s SUR (Parks 1967; Zellner 1962; Wooldridge 2010; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 5.2.1, pp. 127–128). It allows any within-unit heteroskedasticity and serial correlation, rules out cross-sectional correlation, and needs \(N \gg T\) because it estimates \(T(T+1)/2\) covariances from N residual vectors (Croissant and Millo 2019, 128). On a wide short panel it is cheap; on ten firms over twenty years it is 210 parameters from ten observations, and the chapter shows that fit only to read it as unreliable. Driscoll and Kraay note that the shortage of degrees of freedom makes the estimate near-singular and the standard errors downward biased; Beck and Katz document the same small-sample bias in the pooled time series it was first used on (Driscoll and Kraay 1998; Beck and Katz 1995; Croissant and Millo 2019, 128). On within-transformed data the same recipe is Kiefer’s fixed-effects GLS, with one period dropped because the demeaned residual covariance has rank \(T - 1\) (Kiefer 1980; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 5.2.1.2, p. 131); on first differences it is first-difference GLS, the better choice when the fixed-effects residuals are not stationary (Croissant and Millo 2019, 132). plm::pggls fits all three, and the estimated \(\hat\Sigma_T\) in $sigma is itself a picture of the error: off-diagonals that stay flat with distance are a unit effect, off-diagonals that shrink with distance are an AR(1) (Croissant and Millo 2019, 129).
Heteroskedasticity has one more consequence in this book: under it the maximum-likelihood spatial estimators of chapter 03 are inconsistent, and the GM fit is the one to keep (spatial fixed effects; (Lin and Lee 2010; Pesaran 2015, 807)).

title: Appendix K — The error of a panel regression
text:
K.5 4. No memory
Every test here has to decide what to do about the unit effect, and the answer sorts them into three kinds: joint tests of both departures at once, marginal tests of one that assume the other away, and conditional tests of one that allow the other at any size (Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 4.3.2, pp. 96–97). A marginal test for serial correlation that assumes no unit effect will reject because of the unit effect; a joint test rejects for either reason and does not say which.
Baltagi and Li derived the joint Lagrange multiplier test from pooled OLS residuals \(\hat u\). With \(A = \hat u'(I_N \otimes J_T)\hat u / \hat u'\hat u - 1\), the Breusch–Pagan ingredient, and \(B = \hat u'\hat u_{-1} / \hat u'\hat u\), the first-order autocorrelation of the stacked residuals,
\[
LM_1 = \frac{NT^2}{2(T-1)(T-2)} \left[ A^2 - 4AB + 2TB^2 \right]
  \;\sim\; \chi^2_2
\]
under \(H_0: \sigma^2_\alpha = 0,\ \rho = 0\), and the statistic is the same whether the alternative is AR(1) or MA(1) (Baltagi and Li 1991, 1995; Baltagi 2021, eq. 5.36, pp. 125–126). The \(A^2\) term alone is the Breusch–Pagan test, \(LM_2 = \sqrt{NT/2(T-1)}\, A\) in Honda’s one-sided form; the \(B^2\) term alone is the Breusch–Godfrey test on the stacked residuals, \(LM_3 = \sqrt{NT^2/(T-1)}\, B\), which assumes no unit effect (Breusch and Pagan 1980; Honda 1985; Breusch 1978; Godfrey 1978; Baltagi 2021, 126). The cross term \(-4AB\) is why the joint test is needed when both are suspected. And \(LM_3\) is the one not to use: with a unit effect present “one is very likely to reject the null hypothesis of \(H_3\) even if the null is true. This is because the \(\mu_i\) are correlated for the same individual across time, and this will contribute to rejecting the null of no serial correlation” (Baltagi 2021, 127). On Grunfeld it is 143.5 against the locally robust value 10.3 (Baltagi 2021, Table 5.3, p. 129) and the conditional value 69.5 that the chapter prints; both tests are defined below.
Two families fix the marginal tests. The conditional test \(LM_4\) tests \(\rho = 0\) given \(\sigma^2_\alpha > 0\), from the residuals of the random-effects model estimated by maximum likelihood, and is again the same for AR(1) and MA(1) (Baltagi and Li 1995; Baltagi 2021, 127); it is plm::pbltest, and it is the optimal test when a random effect is taken for granted (Croissant and Millo 2019, 97). Bera, Sosa-Escudero and Yoon keep the OLS residuals and correct each marginal statistic for its asymptotic correlation with the other score,
\[
LM^*_\alpha = \frac{NT\,(2B - A)^2}{2(T-1)(1 - 2/T)}, \qquad
LM^*_\rho = \frac{NT^2\,[B - A/T]^2}{(T-1)(1 - 2/T)},
\]
each \(\chi^2_1\) under its null and robust to a small amount of the other departure; the four pieces add up, \(LM^*_\alpha + LM_\rho = LM^*_\rho +
LM_\alpha = LM_1\), so the joint statistic decomposes into an adjusted test of one direction plus the unadjusted test of the other (Bera et al. 2001; Baltagi 2021, 128). These are plm::pbsytest with test = "re", "ar" and "j", and Stata’s xttest1 prints the whole family: on Grunfeld, 798.16 and 28.25 for the unit effect, 664.95 and 25.79 adjusted; 143.52 for serial correlation unadjusted and 10.31 adjusted; 808.47 joint (Baltagi 2021, Table 5.3, p. 129). All of them assume normal, homoskedastic errors (Croissant and Millo 2019, 97).
The fixed-effects test uses within residuals \(\tilde\varepsilon_{it}\), whose unit effect is gone:
\[
LM_5 = \sqrt{\frac{NT^2}{T-1}} \;
  \frac{\tilde\varepsilon' \tilde\varepsilon_{-1}}
       {\tilde\varepsilon' \tilde\varepsilon}
  \;\sim\; N(0, 1)
\]
one-sided, for large T (Baltagi and Li 1995; Baltagi 2021, eq. 5.43, p. 130). It differs from \(LM_3\) only in the residuals, and “since the Within transformation wipes out the individual effects whether fixed or random, one can also use (5.43) to test for serial correlation in the random effects models” (Baltagi 2021, 130). Nothing in plm is literally this statistic; plm::pbgtest on a within fit is its Breusch–Godfrey cousin, and the induced \(-1/(T-1)\) of section 1 biases both toward rejection when T is short (Croissant and Millo 2019, 101). The Bhargava, Franzini and Narendranathan Durbin–Watson is the same residuals in Durbin–Watson form,
\[
d_p = \frac{\sum_i \sum_{t=2}^{T}
             (\tilde\varepsilon_{it} - \tilde\varepsilon_{i,t-1})^2}
           {\sum_i \sum_{t=1}^{T} \tilde\varepsilon_{it}^2},
\]
locally most powerful invariant near \(\rho = 0\), with tabulated bounds for balanced panels and, for very large N, the rule of simply asking whether \(d_p < 2\) (Bhargava et al. 1982; Baltagi 2021, eq. 5.44, p. 130). Baltagi and Wu’s locally best invariant statistic extends it to unequally spaced panels (Baltagi and Wu 1999; Baltagi 2021, 121); plm::pbnftest returns both without a p-value, as Stata does (Baltagi 2021, 130). Inoue and Solon’s portmanteau test of all \((T-1)(T-2)/2\) autocorrelations at once needs \(N \gg T^2/2\) and is not run here (Inoue and Solon 2006; Baltagi 2021, 131).
Wooldridge’s tests need no normality. The unobserved-effects test averages the off-diagonal products of a unit’s pooled residuals, scales by their standard deviation, and is \(N(0, 1)\) as N grows under any error distribution; it has power against a unit effect and against serial correlation alike, “trading some power against more specific alternatives in exchange for robustness”, and a rejection “should not be interpreted as implying that the random effects error structure must be true” (Wooldridge 2010; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 4.3.1, pp. 95–96). The within-based test regresses within residuals on their lag, with an intercept,
\[
\tilde\varepsilon_{it} = \delta + \phi\, \tilde\varepsilon_{i,t-1} + \xi_{it},
\qquad H_0: \phi = -\tfrac{1}{T-1},
\]
with a cluster-robust covariance, so it is valid for short T and large N (Wooldridge 2010; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 4.3.5.1, p. 102). The first-difference test regresses differenced residuals on their lag and tests \(\phi = -0.5\), the value uncorrelated original errors imply; Drukker’s Monte Carlo documents its size and power (Drukker 2003; Wooldridge 2010; Croissant and Millo 2019, 103). Run both ways, h0 = "fe" and h0 = "fd", it is a choice of estimator: if the original errors are white noise, within is efficient and the differenced errors show \(-0.5\); if the original errors are a random walk, the differenced errors are white noise and first differences are efficient (Wooldridge 2010; Baltagi 2021, 22–23; Croissant and Millo 2019, 103). “Not rejecting one of the two is evidence in favor of using the estimator corresponding to h0”; when both reject, “the truth clearly lies in the middle” and “whichever estimator is chosen will have serially correlated errors”, which is the case for robust standard errors (Croissant and Millo 2019, 104).

title: Appendix K — The error of a panel regression
section: K.6 5. The sandwich and its building blocks
text:
K.6 5. The sandwich and its building blocks
Every robust covariance in the chapter is one formula. For a regression with regressors \(X\) and residuals \(\hat u\), the variance of the OLS slopes with a general error covariance is \((X'X)^{-1} (X'\Omega X) (X'X)^{-1}\), and White’s insight is that the middle, the meat, needs only \(K(K+1)/2\) consistent numbers, not the \(NT(NT+1)/2\) in \(\Omega\) (White 1980; Croissant and Millo 2019, sec. 5.1.1, p. 110). The panel estimators differ only in which residual products they let into the meat (Millo 2017):
\[
\begin{aligned}
V_{wh} &= (X'X)^{-1}
  \Big[ \sum_i \sum_t \hat u_{it}^2\, x_{it} x_{it}' \Big] (X'X)^{-1}, \\
V_{cx} &= (X'X)^{-1}
  \Big[ \sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i' \hat u_i \hat u_i' X_i \Big] (X'X)^{-1}, \\
V_{ct} &= (X'X)^{-1}
  \Big[ \sum_{t=1}^{T} X_t' \hat u_t \hat u_t' X_t \Big] (X'X)^{-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\(V_{wh}\) allows the variances to differ and nothing else (Croissant and Millo 2019, eq. 5.4, p. 111). \(V_{cx}\) clusters by unit: it allows any heteroskedasticity and any serial correlation inside a unit, assumes units independent, and is Arellano’s estimator of section 3, Liang and Zeger’s in the statistics literature; its asymptotics are in N, the number of clusters (Arellano 1987; Liang and Zeger 1986; Croissant and Millo 2019, eq. 5.2, p. 111). \(V_{ct}\) clusters by year: any cross-sectional correlation inside a year, years independent, asymptotics in T (Croissant and Millo 2019, eq. 5.5, p. 111). “As a general rule, the estimator is asymptotic in the number of clusters” (Croissant and Millo 2019, 110): ten firms are ten clusters, and the Arellano standard errors on Grunfeld are noisy for that reason.
Double clustering adds the two and subtracts the diagonal that both counted,
\[
V_{cxt} = V_{cx} + V_{ct} - V_{wh},
\]
robust to any dependence within a unit and within a year at once, with the smaller of the two cluster counts having to grow (Cameron et al. 2011; Thompson 2011; Petersen 2009; Croissant and Millo 2019, eq. 5.6, p. 115). It rules out correlation between different units in different years. The kernel estimators let that in, with weights that fall with the lag. Panel Newey–West adds to \(V_{wh}\) the lagged products of each unit’s own residuals,
\[
V_{nw,L} = V_{wh} + \sum_{l=1}^{L} w_l \big[ V_{wh,l} + V_{wh,l}' \big],
\]
with Bartlett weights \(w_l = 1 - l/(L+1)\) and \(L\) of the order of \(T^{1/4}\) (Newey and West 1987; Croissant and Millo 2019, eq. 5.10, pp. 110, 116, 119). Driscoll–Kraay does the same to the year-clustered estimator,
\[
V_{scc,L} = V_{ct} + \sum_{l=1}^{L} w_l \big[ V_{ct,l} + V_{ct,l}' \big],
\]
so that cross-sectional correlation within a year and cross-serial correlation between any two units up to \(L\) years apart are both covered (Driscoll and Kraay 1998; Croissant and Millo 2019, eq. 5.11, p. 116). Its price is the one the spatial chapter’s limits already met: Driscoll and Kraay’s conditions deliver standard errors “robust to general forms of spatial and temporal dependence as \(T \to \infty\). However, if T is small, they conclude that the problem of consistent nonparametric covariance matrix estimation is much less tractable” (Baltagi 2021, 394); the practical minimum from their Monte Carlo is \(T > 20\)–\(25\), and N can grow at any rate (Croissant and Millo 2019, 116). Seventeen and twenty years sit at that floor. Beck and Katz’s panel-corrected standard errors take a different route to the same dependence: assume the \(N \times N\) cross-sectional covariance is the same in every year, estimate it as \(\sum_t \hat u_t \hat u_t' / T\), and plug it into the sandwich; robust to cross-sectional heteroskedasticity and correlation, and only to them (Beck and Katz 1995; Croissant and Millo 2019, eq. 5.13, p. 122).
Millo’s comprehensive formula holds all of these,
\[
V_{cxt,L} = V_{ct} + \sum_{l=1}^{L} w_l [V_{ct,l} + V_{ct,l}']
  + V_{cx} - V_{wh} - \sum_{l=1}^{L} w_l [V_{wh,l} + V_{wh,l}'],
\]
and each named estimator is a choice of which terms to keep and which weights to use: \(L = 0\) gives double clustering, dropping \(V_{cx} - V_{wh}\) and its lags gives Driscoll–Kraay, \(w_l = 1\) gives Thompson’s double clustering with persistent shocks (Millo 2017; Croissant and Millo 2019, eq. 5.12 and Table 5.1, p. 117). plm::vcovG builds one block, vcovHC, vcovSCC, vcovNW and vcovDC are the named sums, and the chapter’s se_table() lays the nine out side by side after every call has been shown. The blocks are additive, so the table reads as a diagnosis: the gap between \(V_{wh}\) and \(V_{cx}\) is serial correlation within a unit, the gap between \(V_{cx}\) and \(V_{cxt}\) is what clustering by year adds, and a kernel estimator that comes out below the clustered one is not reassurance but bias, because the kernel “unduly downweighs the covariance between faraway observations” when the dependence is a persistent unit effect (Petersen 2009; Croissant and Millo 2019, 119–21).
Two cautions on transformed data. The within transformation induces the \(-1/(T-1)\) correlation of section 1, so clustering by unit with unit effects is right, clustering by year with time effects is right, and “the combination of group clustering with time fixed effects and the reverse is inappropriate” (Croissant and Millo 2019, 121). And a persistent unit effect left in the residuals biases every kernel estimator, which is one reason to demean or difference before applying one (Croissant and Millo 2019, 121).

title: Appendix K — The error of a panel regression
text:
K.7 If / then







If
Then




Chow’s F rejects but the errors have a unit effect
The plain F over-rejects; read the Roy–Zellner F on the GLS-transformed data (Baltagi 2021, 79)


The slopes differ and N is large against T
Swamy’s \(\chi^2\) needs \(T \to \infty\) at fixed N; the Δ tests are the right ones and are not in R (Pesaran 2015, 737–39)


\(\hat\Delta\) is not positive definite
Report the mean-group dispersion, which always is (Croissant and Millo 2019, 190)


Residual spread grows with unit size
Slopes stay consistent; replace the classical errors by Arellano’s, or reweight by FGLS if \(N \gg T\) (Baltagi 2021, 18–19, 109; Croissant and Millo 2019, 128)


Only the unit effect is in doubt
Breusch–Pagan or Honda; \(LM_3\) never, since the unit effect makes it reject (Baltagi 2021, 127)


Both departures are suspected
The joint \(LM_1\), then the BSY adjusted pair to say which (Baltagi 2021, 128)


A random effect is taken as given
The conditional \(LM_4\) from the ML fit (Croissant and Millo 2019, 97)


The model is fixed effects
Within residuals: \(LM_5\), BFN’s \(d_p\), or Wooldridge’s within test against \(-1/(T-1)\) (Baltagi 2021, 130; Croissant and Millo 2019, 102)


h0 = "fe" rejects and h0 = "fd" does not
First differences; the original errors look like a random walk (Croissant and Millo 2019, 103–4)


Both legs of the FD test reject
Either estimator with a serial-correlation-robust covariance (Croissant and Millo 2019, 104)


Dependence is within units only
Cluster by unit; asymptotics in N (Croissant and Millo 2019, 111)


Dependence is within years and within units
Double clustering; both counts must be large (Croissant and Millo 2019, 115)


Units are correlated across years too, and \(T > 20\)–\(25\)
Driscoll–Kraay (Croissant and Millo 2019, 116; Baltagi 2021, 394)


A kernel estimator is smaller than the clustered one
The unit effect is persistent and the kernel is biased; trust the cluster (Croissant and Millo 2019, 121)

title: Appendix K — The error of a panel regression
text:
K.8 Open

Pesaran–Yamagata Δ and its HAC extension have no R implementation; Stata’s xthst is the benchmark, and the chapter defers it (Bersvendsen and Ditzen 2021; Blomquist and Westerlund 2013).
Verbon’s and Lejeune’s tests of homoskedasticity, and the joint LM test of Baltagi, Bresson and Pirotte that nests them, are not implemented; the chapter has a picture and a substitute, not a test with a published size (Baltagi et al. 2006; Baltagi 2021, 113–14).
\(LM_5\) is not literally in plm; pbnftest and pbgtest on within residuals are the nearest (Baltagi 2021, 130).
Bester, Conley and Hansen’s group-membership HAC estimator is not implemented; its validity “relies on the capacity of the researcher to construct groups whose averages are approximately uncorrelated”, and plm::cortab checks that precondition and nothing more (Bester et al. 2011; Pesaran 2015, 814).
Inoue–Solon needs \(N \gg T^2/2\) and is not run on any panel here (Baltagi 2021, 131).

title: Appendix K — The error of a panel regression
text:
K.9 Next
When the errors are nearer a random walk than white noise, the regression itself is the problem, not its standard errors, and the lagged outcome belongs on the right-hand side: dynamic panel GMM. The unit effect that every test here had to allow for is the subject of fixed and random effects.
